activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
Riley had been to his grandmother's house every December since before he could remember, but he had never seen the basement table dressed the way it was dressed now: a woven mat, an ear of dried corn, a candleholder with three red candles, one black, and three green, all still unlit. His grandmother moved a stack of hymnals off the sideboard and set down a tall tapered candle, then looked at him the way she looked at him when she had already decided something.

"You're going to open it tonight," she said. "Second generation gets the second candle."

Riley knew what she meant and also didn't. His father had started keeping Kwanzaa two years ago, after the year they didn't talk about, and the family had gone along with it in the way families go along with things, with raised eyebrows and extra casseroles. Riley had eaten the food, said the words after everyone else said them, and absorbed nothing. Now his grandmother was handing him a folded piece of paper, and his father was carrying the kinarа down to the table with the carefulness of a man holding a live coal, and Riley understood that in about forty minutes he would be standing in front of his aunts and uncles and small cousins, expected to speak.

He ducked into the kitchen and called Zakariya, who kept Kwanzaa properly, whose whole house kept it, and who answered on the second ring with the sound of pots behind him. "It's Umoja tonight," Zakariya said. "First day, first principle. It runs December twenty-sixth through January first, so tonight's the opening. Dr. Maulana Karenga created the whole thing back in 1966. Seven days, seven principles, one for each day, and Umoja comes first." Riley wrote umoja on the back of his grandmother's grocery list and asked how to say it. Zakariya said it twice, oo-MOH-ja, and then someone on his end called him away and the call ended before Riley could ask the question he actually wanted to ask, which was what you were supposed to do if you weren't sure you believed any of it.

He tried to look it up, but the basement swallowed the signal, so he sat on the bottom stair with the grocery list and worked from memory. Unity. One candle, one word, a holiday younger than his grandmother and younger than his father, invented by a man whose name Riley would not have recognized a week ago. He felt a flicker of foreboding, the specific kind that comes before speaking in front of relatives, and under it something harder to name, a suspicion that the whole ceremony was a costume the family had put on because the real thing, the older thing, the church on Christmas morning thing, had stopped fitting his father somewhere along the way. He could impute that motive to his dad, sure. People at school imputed worse, he had seen a comment thread over the holiday turn vitriolic about Kwanzaa and about people who kept it and about people who didn't, everyone certain, everyone furious, and Riley had closed the tab without typing anything.

In the living room the chairs had been arranged in a circle. His grandmother lit the black candle first, then handed him the taper for the first red one, and the flame took slowly, the wick hissing, a smell like struck matches climbing toward the ceiling. Somebody's baby made a delighted noise. His father's face in the candlelight was open in a way Riley hadn't seen since before the year they didn't talk about.

"Umoja," Riley said, and his voice cracked on the second syllable and a cousin giggled and he kept going anyway. "Unity. It's the first of seven principles, one for each of the seven nights, and it means staying one thing together even when it's easier to come apart." He looked at his grandmother, then at his father, then at his shoes. "I didn't know all that an hour ago. I called a friend. I'm telling you that because I think it matters that we're all still learning it, and I don't want to stand here and pretend I've got something figured out that I don't." It was not the speech his father had probably imagined. It was not the speech Riley had imagined either. But when he sat down, his grandmother's hand found the back of his neck and stayed there, warm, unmoving, through the whole next part.

Afterward there was food, and his uncle made a joke about the corn, and his father came to stand next to him at the folding table where the red punch was. Riley waited for the correction, the lecture, the disappointed silence. Instead his father put a cup in his hand and said, "Karenga. Zakariya told you." Riley said yeah. His father nodded slowly, watching the candle burn itself lower across the room, and said, "Six more nights. You want day three, or should I give it to Katherine?" Riley thought of Katherine texting him about chemistry homework, of the seven words he'd learned and the ones he hadn't, of the way the family had rearranged its chairs into a circle for something none of them fully understood yet. He took a drink of the punch, which was too sweet, and said, "I'll take three. What is it?"

His father smiled, and the candle guttered once in the draft from the kitchen door, and then steadied.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
Autumn was not nervous about the interview, which is why she had practiced her handshake on the doorframe twice and had recited her answers into the bathroom mirror while the sauerkraut fermented on the counter behind her, its smell seeping under the door like a fact she could not argue with. The interview was Saturday at Delgado's, the sandwich place near the hardware store, and she wanted the job the way you want something you have decided you deserve. She had written out answers to the usual questions, folded the paper into eighths, and brought it to dinner, where her father was serving the sauerkraut with sausage and where Braden had been invited because his mother worked late on Thursdays.

"Tell me about yourself," her father said, pointing his fork at her. He enjoyed this. He put on a voice like a magistrate delivering sentence, which he seemed to think was what interviewers did. Autumn gave her prepared answer, the one about being responsible and punctual and good with people, and she kept her eyes on his the whole time, which was the point, because Ms. Addo next door had told her that the whole interview was decided in the first ninety seconds and that eye contact was most of it.

"You blinked," said her little brother, who did not matter and whose name is not worth recording.

"I did not blink," Autumn said, and she had not, technically, although her eyes had watered so badly that the kitchen had gone smeary, which she chose not to classify as blinking.

Braden was pushing kraut around his plate. He had a job already, at the grocery by the school, and Autumn assumed he was there to be outshone, which was fine with her. "They're going to ask why you want to work at a sandwich shop," he said. "You can't say money."

"Why not. It's money."

"It's, like, the wrong genre."

Her mother said the interview would be good experience regardless, in the way that adults say things that mean nothing, and Autumn nodded and gave an answer so equivocal that even she could not later recall what she had said, something about growth and opportunity. Then Braden said the thing that rearranged the evening.

"You know Delgado's has the deli counter," he said. "The guy who's leaving was my brother's friend. He ran the slicer."

"The meat slicer," said her father, with the pleasure of a man who knows something is about to be significant.

Autumn set down her fork. She had read about this, actually, three weeks ago, at two in the morning, in one of those spirals where you look up labor laws instead of sleeping. Sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds had no limit on hours, none, you could work forty a week or more if the employer allowed it, but the Department of Labor had declared certain jobs hazardous, and a meat slicer was one of them, and the rules did not care that she was careful, or almost seventeen, or that her mother had let her use the table saw in the garage. She had filed it away as trivia. Now it sat on the table between the sausage and the kraut.

"Then they can't schedule me on it," she said. "It's not allowed. But everything else, the register, the prep, the closing shifts, that's all legal. There's literally no cap on hours at my age." She heard herself lecturing and did not entirely stop.

"So you'd be the only one who can't do the slicer," Braden said. "The new person. The one who can't."

The kitchen went quiet except for the crock of fermenting cabbage doing whatever it did in the corner. Her little brother said, "You blinked again," and she had, and this time she let it stand. Here was the thing she had not worked out: she could walk into Delgado's on Saturday with her practiced handshake and her steady eyes and ask, up front, about the slicer, and be honest and informed and possibly annoying. Or she could say nothing, take the job, and trust that a sandwich shop would follow the law without her mentioning it, which was the kind of trust that had never once worked out for anyone in her family.

"I'll ask," she said. "First thing. Clear answer, eye contact."

"Bold," said Braden.

Her father raised his glass of water to her like a magistrate acknowledging, at last, a worthy witness, and her mother said, "Then eat your sausage, you'll need it," and Autumn looked down at her plate and realized she had finished it already, every bite, without noticing a single one.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
Hannah had missed four games, and the doctor's sheet in her back pocket had six lines on it, each one a step.

She had learned the order by heart without meaning to. Rest came first, then light activity, then sport-specific work without contact, then full practice, then game play. You moved up one line only if you stayed free of symptoms, and if a symptom came back you dropped a line and started again from there. Coach Reyes kept the sheet taped inside the first-aid kit, but Hannah had her own copy because the season was short and every Tuesday the team trained on the field behind the school, and she wanted to be on it.

At Tuesday practice she was on line three: drills, no contact, no heading the ball. She jogged the warm-up laps with Saphira, who talked the whole way about a party she was not invited to, and then Ms. Chowdhury, who taught chemistry and coached the girls in the fall, split them into stations. Hannah took crosses from the wing and laid them back, again and again, the ball arriving soft and leaving softer, and she felt fine. She felt so fine that she began to think the whole protocol was a kind of artifice, a bureaucratic hedge designed to protect adults from lawsuits, and that her real self, the one who could slide tackle in the mud, was being kept in a drawer.

"Line four next week if you're good," Ms. Chowdhury said, and Hannah said, "I'm good now," and Ms. Chowdhury only looked at her and moved down the touchline.

Rylee had been on the team since Hannah was a freshman, and Rylee had taken a knee to the temple in the second game of the season. Rylee was on line two, light activity, jogging and passing at walking pace, nothing faster. Hannah had watched her climb the ladder over three weeks, from her bedroom with the curtains drawn, to the easy laps, to this. Now Rylee was running the passing pattern at the far end, and Hannah could see that she was going too hard. Her touches were sharper than the drill asked for, and she kept glancing over at the scrimmage in the middle of the field as though the glance itself could move her there.

Halfway through the second set Rylee stopped. She stood with her hands on her knees, then straightened, then pressed the heel of her hand against her forehead just above her left eyebrow. She walked to the sideline without being called and sat down on the cooler.

Hannah jogged over. The evening light lay flat across the alluvial grass near the drainage ditch, where silt collected after every hard rain and the ground stayed soft months longer than the rest of the field, and Rylee sat at the edge of that softness with her eyes shut.

"Headache," Rylee said. "It went away Monday. It's back."

"Back how?"

"Like before. Behind my eye."

Hannah crouched. She wanted to say it was nothing, that everyone got headaches in August heat, and part of her believed it, the same part that had called the protocol a hedge. But the sheet was specific. You moved up only while you stayed free of symptoms, and a returning headache was a symptom, and so the direction of Rylee's week had just reversed itself. "You're back down a step," Hannah said. "That's how it works, right? A step back until it's gone again."

"I know how it works." Rylee opened her eyes. "I did three weeks."

"You did three weeks and you'll do them better the second time, because you already know the ladder."

Rylee laughed without any sound in it. "You're one to talk. You've been trying to talk Chowdhury into skipping you ahead since the day you got cleared for contact drills."

Ms. Chowdhury came over with her water bottle and asked Rylee the questions she asked, and Rylee answered them, and then Ms. Chowdhury said, "You're back at line two tomorrow, and we'll hold you there till you're clean," and Rylee nodded and kept her hand over her eyebrow.

Hannah stood in the soft grass and thought about the two things she had been carrying. One was the belief that the rules were padding around people who could not judge their own limits. The other was the fact of Rylee's hand on her forehead, and the fact of her own copy of the sheet, folded into eighths, carried daily like a confession. She could not make them into one clean idea. Maybe the rules were a hedge and Rylee still needed the hedge. Maybe honesty about the body was something you could not feel your way to, only count your way to, one line at a time, and that felt less like weakness than like arithmetic.

She took the sheet out of her pocket and unfolded it on her knee. Line four said full practice, contact included, and next Tuesday was nine days away.

"Give me your copy," Rylee said from the cooler. "Mine's in my other bag."

Hannah held it out, and Rylee smoothed it flat against her shin guard, studied the six lines for a long moment, and then said, "Coach. I'm cleared through line three. Can I do Hannah's station?"

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Isla had a clipboard, a whistle she was afraid to use, and eleven twelve-year-olds who could not complete a chest pass to save their lives. She had taken the coaching job because Ms. Sultani needed someone for the junior team and Isla needed something that looked like leadership on her college applications, a fact she was not proud of but also not prepared to eulogize in public. The gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn. The kids were already scrimmaging badly, the ball pinwheeling out of bounds every fourth possession.

Her first instinct was to fix everything immediately. "Elbows in, Maya, step into it." "Follow through, Dev." "Soft hands, softer, softer." She called out something after nearly every pass, and for the first week it seemed to be working. The drills looked cleaner. Linda, her assistant and best friend since grade four, kept a tally on her phone and reported that completion rates had climbed from terrible to merely embarrassing. Linda's actual ambition, which she mentioned roughly twice per practice, was to be named head coach of the summer program, so she cared about the numbers the way a lawyer cares about a subpoena: anxiously, and with documents.

Then they played their first real game against the middle school across town, and Isla watched her team fall apart like a sweater pulled loose at the cuff. The same kids who had passed crisply in practice threw the ball to nobody, to the wrong team, once directly into the bleachers. Maya caught a pass and then just stood there, waiting, her eyes drifting to the sideline where Isla was not saying anything because there was nothing yet to say. They lost by nineteen points. On the bus home Linda said, "They were looking for you before they even caught the ball," and Isla, staring out the window, had to admit it was true.

She spent Sunday with her mother's old motor learning textbook, which she'd dug out of the basement after remembering a unit from psychology class. She found a paragraph about feedback and read it three times. The following morning she cornered Martha, who was shooting free throws alone in the gym before school, and read the paragraph aloud.

"Oh, that's the guidance hypothesis," Martha said, wiping her face with her shirt. "We covered it. Feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it. Less frequent feedback often helps retention." She spun the ball on one finger, ruined it immediately, and chased it across the lane. "Why, did you murder a twelve-year-old's confidence?"

"Legally I cannot answer that without a subpoena," Isla said, and Martha laughed so hard she missed her next shot, which was florid in its badness, an arc of pure tragedy, off the backboard and over everything.

So Isla changed her plan, and it cost her something to do it, because staying quiet felt like neglect. She designed drills for the specific weakness, the passing, but she held her tongue. Ten passes, then one comment. Sometimes ten passes, then nothing, just a nod. Linda protested at first, wanting the visible correction, the coachly performance of it, something she could put in a report to Ms. Sultani. "They're going to think we don't care," she said. "They're going to think you've given up."

"I think I was the one giving them something they can't take onto the court," Isla said, and heard how uncertain it came out, because she was uncertain. Maybe it was her. Maybe the kids were just twelve and doomed. She held up the tally phone. "New rule. You count passes, I talk every tenth one. If the numbers don't move in two weeks, you can fire me and take the clipboard."

The numbers moved. Slowly, unglamorously, with a relapse in week two when they all caught a collective case of the dropsies, the completion rate climbed, and Isla learned the harder half of the lesson, which was that the silence had to be filled by the kids themselves. Maya started talking on the court. Dev started correcting his own feet. In the rematch across town, the score stayed close until the final minute, and when Maya threw a skip pass across the key to a girl whose name Isla had honestly never learned, the girl caught it and laid it in, and none of them looked at the sideline even once.

Afterward, in the emptying gym, Linda handed over the clipboard. Not for keeps, just to hold the door while she gathered the cones, but she let the moment sit there a second longer than necessary, and Isla understood she was being trusted with something larger than cones. Ms. Sultani passed by with the ball bag over her shoulder and said, "Same time Thursday," and Isla said, "Same time Thursday," and tucked the clipboard under her arm like she'd been carrying it for years.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: The margin of error measures only random sampling error; it does not cover errors from badly worded questions, people refusing to answer, or poorly conducted interviews.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and cold coffee, and by nine in the morning Aaron had already learned that polling stations have their own weather. Voters came in gusts, then nothing for twenty minutes, then a line that bent past the bleachers. He stood near the door with a clipboard and a stack of surveys, counting people the way Ms. Hassan had shown him when she signed him in as the student observer. Every fifth voter, she had said, and don't chase the ones who wave you off.

The deadline was noon. The school paper, The Ledger, went to layout at one, and Ricardo was already texting him from the newsroom, where he was building a page around the headline STUDENTS PREDICT SCHOOL BOARD RACE. Aaron's exit poll was supposed to fill the front-page box with numbers. Two hundred and forty respondents, a sample size he'd chosen himself, because a bigger sample meant a smaller margin of error, and a smaller margin of error meant the numbers could be trusted. That was the whole logic of the morning.

Caleigh arrived at ten with her own clipboard and a thermos she kept refilling from the water fountain. She was voluble before caffeine and nearly unstoppable after it, narrating each voter's probable choices based on their coats. She had written the survey question at eleven the night before, in the group chat, and Aaron had approved it without reading closely because he was formatting the spreadsheet. "Should the board keep wasting money on the stadium instead of classrooms?" She'd polled sixty people with it by the time he saw what it said.

"It's a little leading," he said, keeping his voice low near Ms. Hassan's table.

"It's accurate," Caleigh said. "The stadium is a waste. And look, I checked the math. Sixty people, margin of error, plus or minus. That's the error. It's in the name."

He wanted to believe her, mostly because the numbers were dramatic: seventy percent against the stadium, which would make the story easy. He watched a man in a canvas jacket refuse Caleigh's clipboard with a raised palm, then accept a ballot and vote anyway, and something about that small refusal bothered him more than the question did. The man would never appear in the sample. Neither would the woman who had answered the door of the gymnasium of Aaron's attention with a shrug and "I don't talk to kids about politics." The ones who waved you off, Ms. Hassan had said, and she'd said it like it was ordinary weather.

At eleven fifteen Ricardo called. "Numbers, Aaron. Where are my numbers."

"Forty more minutes."

"We don't have forty minutes. Layout's moving it up. Caleigh's sixty with the stadium question, that's a box, we can run that."

Aaron found Ms. Hassan refilling the tape on a signage stand and asked, quietly, whether a margin of error covered a question that was written to push an answer. She considered him for a second, then said only, "The margin of error measures one kind of error," and went back to her tape, which was the closest thing to a reprimand she ever gave. He stood there doing the arithmetic she'd left him with. Random sampling error, the kind that shrank as the sample grew. Not the question's wording. Not the refusals. Not Caleigh rushing a man in a hurry this morning, reading the options to him fast, writing down something the man hadn't exactly said.

He had two kinds of counting in his head and he had been treating them as the same thing. The sample size controlled the noise, and he'd let it stand guard over everything else, the way you habituate to a bad smell in a room you work in. The wording was a confounder, except that word made it sound fancy and structural when really it was just Caleigh wanting to be right, and himself wanting a front page, and both of them being seventeen and quick.

At eleven forty he told Ricardo the stadium number was out. There was shouting from the phone, tinny, the kind of shouting that ends in "fine, fine, we'll run it without the box." Caleigh stood with her clipboard against her chest and said the question was fine, and then, quieter, asked which part was wrong, the question or the people who wouldn't answer it, and Aaron said both, and neither, and that he didn't have a number for how wrong. He kept his own tally going for the last twenty minutes, clean question, every fifth voter, and watched the count land near fifty-two percent, close enough to the margin of error that the race could go either way, which was, he thought, the most honest box the paper could print.

At noon Ms. Hassan walked him to the door and asked if he'd learned anything worth the morning. A woman in a green coat was signing in behind them, and the pen ran dry mid-signature, and Ms. Hassan shook a fresh one without looking. "Ask her," Aaron said. "If she'll answer."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Ricardo's original model treats labor as the only cost of production and assumes that cost stays the same however much of a good is made.
story:
Michael had the essay half written in his head by the time he pushed the cart through the sliding doors, which was exactly the kind of thing he told himself when he hadn't written a word of it. It was due at midnight. It was now a little after eight.

The assignment was Mr. Tehrani's, and Mr. Tehrani had a way of circling a sentence in red and writing "says who?" beside it that made Michael want to be right before he typed. The prompt asked them to explain comparative advantage, why two countries both gain from trading even when one of them is better at everything, and then, before criticizing the model, to list the simplifying assumptions behind Ricardo's example. Michael had the first part down. The second part he had avoided for three days.

Lexi worked the register on aisle four, and he had promised to trade her a shift walk-through for help. She was on break in ten minutes, she'd texted, and she wanted his calculus notes as payment, tonight, because her exam was tomorrow morning. He was the only person in their grade who annotated.

He grabbed a basket instead of a cart, since his mother had sent him for olive oil, dish soap, and the recalcitrant items she always had to list twice because they never seemed to make it home. He put the list in his pocket and walked to the cereal, where the wifi was decent, and opened his laptop against a shelf of oat bins.

Ricardo, England, Portugal, cloth, wine. He could hear Mr. Tehrani's voice saying that the example was older than most countries in the room. Michael typed: "Labor is the only cost of production." He stopped. Was that in the example or was that him smuggling in something he half remembered from a video? He typed underneath it: "and the cost stays the same however much of the good is made," then deleted that, then typed it again, because it felt true in the way things feel true when you're out of time.

Lexi appeared at the end of the aisle with her name tag flipped backward and a basket of her own, which she set on the floor like a suitcase. "Deadline?" she said.

"Midnight. Yours?"

"Eight a.m. review session. Notes."

He handed over the folder. She flipped through it, and he watched her watching it, and he understood that she was checking whether the annotations were real or whether he'd scribbled them in study hall to look like diligence, which was fair, because he had done that once, and she had covered for him, and neither of them had mentioned it since.

"Explain your thing to me," she said. "If you can explain it to me, it's right. That's the test."

"That's not the test."

"It's my test."

He set the laptop on a stack of paper towels. "Okay. Say I'm better than you at both math and washing dishes. Everything. You can't do anything I can't do better."

"Rude, but continue."

"Trade still helps us both if I give up less doing the thing I'm relatively best at. I do the math, you do the dishes, and we're both better off than if we each did everything ourselves. That's the whole idea."

"And Ricardo's version?"

"Countries, cloth, wine." He scrolled to his assumptions list. "But here's what I keep snagging on. In his example labor is the only cost, like there's no machinery, no land, nothing else. And it assumes that cost stays the same however much you make of the good. Every unit costs the same as the first one, forever."

Lexi squinted at the frozen food case across the aisle as if it had said something. "That seems like a lot to assume."

"That's the criticism, though. That's the whole second half of the essay. And I don't want to be the guy who tears down a model for its assumptions when the assumptions are the reason it works at all. Mr. Tehrani hates that. He says we valorize the critique and skip the part where we ask what the model still tells us."

"He said valorize?"

"He says it constantly. It's his whole thing. He told us last week that if he ever became a magistrate he'd sentence every senior to rewriting one paragraph they were sure of."

"That doesn't even mean anything."

"It means being sure is the crime."

Lexi closed the notes folder, and he saw her decide, in the way you see someone decide, that the annotations were real. "So which is it? Do the assumptions break the model or not?"

"I don't know yet. That's the honest answer. It's right about the big thing, the trade part, I believe that. But the constant-cost part, I can't tell if that's a harmless simplification or the load-bearing wall."

The store announcement crackled overhead, aisle five, spill cleanup, and Lexi picked up her basket because her break was over whether the announcement said so or not. "Write both," she said. "Say you don't know. Say what would have to be true for each side to win."

"That's not an essay, that's a shrug."

"It's midnight in four hours. It's a shrug or nothing."

She headed toward the registers, and he stood there between the oat bins and the paper towels with the dish soap forgotten, typing the assumption back in, labor as the only cost, cost the same at every quantity, and then underneath it, in a sentence he underlined twice: whether that honesty about the model's limits was a weakness of the essay or its whole point, he could not yet say.

He picked up the olive oil last and got in her line.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: German historian Alexander Demandt compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell.
story:
Dominic arrived at his aunt's house carrying his half of the argument in his back pocket, folded twice, warm from the bus. The assignment from Ms. Demir had seemed simple: pick a cause for the fall of the Western Roman Empire and defend it in class on Tuesday. He had chosen moral decline, mostly because the sources were vivid, all those writers sneering at luxury and softness while the borders crumbled. He had expected to win the debate easily. He had not expected his uncle to bring it up at the table.

"Rome," his uncle was saying, spearing a potato, "collapsed because of the lead pipes. Poisoned the whole ruling class. Everyone knows it." A cousin disagreed, loudly, about taxation. Somebody's grandfather muttered that it was the barbarians, and had always been the barbarians, and that arguing about it was a modern habit. Dominic sat back and watched the turkey go around, half amused and half sullen that his carefully rehearsed answer was being torn apart by people who had never read a word of Gibbon.

He texted Davin under the table: how many reasons do you think there are for Rome falling. Davin, who was at his own family gathering two streets away, replied almost immediately: my uncle says immigration, my grandma says God. Dominic texted Cierra next, because Cierra read everything and remembered it all. She took longer, and her answer arrived while he was carrying dishes to the kitchen: "A German historian, Alexander Demandt, made a list of 210 different explanations writers have given for why the Western Roman Empire fell."

Dominic stood at the sink with his hands in the soapy water, holding that number. Two hundred and ten. Not two, not five, the tidy handful that a class discussion could weigh and discard. He had internalized a single cause so thoroughly that it had begun to feel like a fact rather than an argument, and now the fact had dissolved into a swarm. What struck him most was not that so many explanations existed but that people kept generating them, century after century, each writer finding in Rome whatever troubled his own time. Lead pipes for an age worried about poison, taxes for an age worried about money, decadence for an age worried about its own appetites.

He turned the idea over while he dried a platter. Suppose every source was partial, written by someone with a grudge or a patron or a sermon to deliver. Suppose the questions themselves changed, so that asking why Rome fell in 1700 was almost a different question from asking it now. His essay on moral decline suddenly looked less like a door and more like a window, one pane among many, facing one direction over a very large landscape.

Back in the dining room the argument had drifted to his uncle's theory of everything, which involved, somehow, the fall of Rome and the present government both being the fault of an oligarchy that cared only for itself. "Always the same story," his uncle said, tapping the tablecloth. "A few families take everything, and then the whole thing comes down." Dominic caught himself before he said that this was, in fact, explanation number something on Demandt's list, presumably alongside lead, plague, climate, Christianity, and two hundred others he could not name. Instead he asked, genuinely curious, "But if two hundred and ten people looked at the same empire and each saw something different, does that mean most of them were wrong? Or that they were all looking at real pieces?"

His uncle blinked at him. "It means people see what they want to see."

"Maybe," Dominic said. "Or maybe an empire that size fell for a hundred reasons at once, and the honest answer is that we can't rank them, because the sources are just... fragments. Whatever survived."

"That's no kind of answer," his uncle said, but he said it more quietly, and he pushed the gravy toward Dominic, which in his uncle's language was something like respect.

In the hallway, pulling on his jacket, Dominic typed a message to Cierra: what if I argue that the real lesson is there's no single cause, that the disagreement is the finding. She replied with a single word, "Careful," and then, "Demandt's list doesn't mean all explanations are equal. Some are just wrong." He read it twice, then a third time while his mother called from the porch that the car was warm and waiting. He hadn't decided anything yet, he realized, and there was something almost pleasant in that, standing in his aunt's doorway with two ideas in either hand and no way yet to make them agree. The porch light flicked on above him. "Dominic," his mother called again, "we're leaving."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The ballot pamphlet had been living in Aaron's backpack for eleven days, folded twice, its edges going soft. On the last Friday before the election, Mr. Anderson set a timer on the whiteboard and told the class they would spend the period arguing whether voting was a duty or a choice, and that anyone who wanted to speak had to claim a side by the bell.

Roger claimed duty before the timer started, because Roger always claimed first and thought after. Charles-Edouard, who had arrived from Lyon in September and treated the class discussions like a sport he was still learning the rules of, claimed choice. That left Aaron with the desk by the window and no side at all, which was more or less how he had felt since he turned eighteen in March and the registration card arrived in an envelope he still hadn't fully opened.

"Here's a thing," Charles-Edouard said, turning around in his seat, his tablet open on his knees. "I was comparing countries last night. In Australia, they've used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925. If you don't vote and you don't have a valid reason, you can be fined."

"No," Roger said. "Fined? For not doing something? They can't fine you for staying home."

"That's what I read. Since 1925, I'm telling you."

Aaron wrote the date in his margin and then, because writing it made it more real, wrote beside it: skipping costs money there, costs nothing here. Mr. Anderson walked the rows listening, hands behind his back, saying nothing, which was his way of making the silence do the teaching.

The argument swept past him. Roger talked about people who died for suffrage, and Charles-Edouard said that forcing a choice devalued it, that a vote extracted under threat was a hollow ritual, and the two of them went back and forth with increasing volume while the timer counted down from twenty minutes. Aaron found he was listening to both of them at once, and that neither position, taken alone, matched anything he actually believed. He believed Roger was right that a democracy runs on participation. He also believed Charles-Edouard was right that a person who votes only to avoid a fine has done something smaller than a person who votes because he means it.

"Your side, Aaron," Mr. Anderson said, stopping at his desk. "You've been quiet."

"I don't have one," Aaron said, and when the class laughed a little, he went on anyway, because it was true. "I think Charles-Edouard's right that a compelled vote isn't worth much. But I think Roger's right that if everyone waited until they felt inspired, nobody would go. So maybe the question isn't duty versus choice. Maybe it's whether I'm the kind of person who lets the boring days decide for him." He heard how it sounded, half philosophy lecture, half confession, and kept going. "There's a word for sitting around asking whether your choices even matter. Existentialism. We read about it. The whole point was that it's not an excuse. It's the opposite."

"Vague," Roger said, but not unkindly.

"Then let me be incisive," Aaron said. "The polls close at six. I'm registered, my card's in my bag, and I still don't know if I'm going. That's not vague. That's my actual problem."

The bell rang before anyone could answer him, and the room emptied the way rooms do, all at once and loudly. Charles-Edouard paused at Aaron's desk on the way out. "In France we have a saying," he began, and then gave up on the saying and just said, "Go vote. Then tell me tomorrow if it felt like a duty or a choice. I'm collecting data."

At home Aaron ate standing up, the pamphlet open beside his plate, and read the arguments one last time. His mother asked from the doorway whether he needed a ride, twice, because he didn't answer the first time. One of the candidates wanted to expropriate a strip of the old rail corridor for a public greenway, and the phrase "expropriate private land" appeared in bold in the pamphlet, and Aaron sat with it, weighing a person's claim to a fence line against a path other people would walk for a hundred years. He did not know the answer. He underlined it twice, then once more.

At five forty he left the house on foot because the polling station was at the elementary school four blocks over and walking gave him nine more minutes of not deciding. The light was going amber over the lawns. At the door, a volunteer with a clipboard looked up at him, pen already moving.

"Name?" she asked.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
story:
Alexandra slid the paycheque stub across the kitchen table so Baby could see it, then pulled it back because the numbers were small and she wanted to read them herself first. Six weeks of Saturdays at the garden centre, and the deposit line was smaller than any of them had guessed. "There's a whole section they took off," she said. "Federal, provincial, then something called CPP, then EI."

"EI?" Pyper leaned over Baby's shoulder, her elbows planted in the ring of water a glass had left on the wood.

"Employment insurance, I think. It's insurance in case I lose the job." Alexandra had spent twenty minutes on the phone with her mother over it, both of them squinting at the same thin paper from different cities. "Gross pay is what I earned. Net pay is what actually lands in my account."

Pyper frowned at the two figures as though the difference had been taken from her personally. "So they malign you with math before you even get the money."

"They don't malign you, they just take it," Baby said. "That's what deductions are."

"It's a contrivance," Pyper said, waving a hand. "The whole thing. They could put the real number on the job posting and they don't."

There was a knock, and Ms. Quinn from next door came in carrying a shoebox of papers, the way she did every April, because Alexandra's mother had told her Alexandra was good with figures. She set the box down and started sorting receipts into little igneous-grey stacks, restaurant, pharmacy, hardware store, without asking anyone to help, though help was clearly the point of coming. Alexandra slid her paycheque stub under the shoebox lid, feeling suddenly that her small losses were too small to mention.

Except she did mention it. "Ms. Quinn, can I ask something? Last week I had exactly enough for the slice at Verona's. Twelve dollars, and the menu says twelve dollars. And the register said more."

"Was it much more?"

"Like eighty cents. Baby had to cover it." She could still feel the heat in her ears, standing at the counter while the cashier waited and the line lengthened behind her. "I had counted it out twice before we left."

Baby nodded slowly. "The menu price wasn't the total. The tax gets added at the register, so what you pay is higher than what's posted."

"Everywhere?" Alexandra looked from Baby to Pyper to Ms. Quinn. "Not just restaurants?"

"Shelf prices too," Baby said. "The sticker on the shelf isn't the final number."

Ms. Quinn held up one of her grey stacks, a fan of restaurant slips, and let Alexandra look. On each one the printed total sat above the listed price, and every total was higher, by a little, by a bit more. Alexandra spread three of them in a row on the table, aligning their edges. It was consistent, that was the thing. Not a trick played on her once, at the one counter where she happened to be short. It was the ordinary shape of every purchase, and she had simply never had reason to see it before, because her mother had always been the one holding the wallet.

"So the posted price is like my gross pay," she said. "The number before the subtractions. Except with the paycheque they tell you they're taking it, and with the pizza they just sort of let you find out."

"It's the reverse, though," Pyper said. "On your paycheque they take away. At the register they add on."

Alexandra turned one of the receipts over, then back, checking whether the added amount appeared anywhere. It did, printed small, a percentage she didn't try to compute in her head. "I don't know which way is more honest," she said. "Telling you up front and then shrinking it, or advertising one number and growing it. Maybe neither one's honest. Maybe honest would be the actual number, everywhere, the number you actually hand over."

Ms. Quinn was quiet for a moment, squaring a stack against the table's edge. "Some places do it that way," she said. "Other countries. But that's all I know about it."

Alexandra picked up her paycheque stub again and looked from it to the receipts and back, the two systems sitting side by side on the table, one shrinking and one swelling, and she understood them together now, though not which one she'd prefer if anyone ever asked her to choose. She lined the stub up with the edge of the receipts.

"Next Saturday," she said, "I'm bringing thirteen dollars to Verona's."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The chair in Ms. Doyle's office had a wobble in it that Evan had never bothered to report, and today he rocked in it deliberately, as though the squeak might fill the silence for him. On the desk between them sat two envelopes, one opened, one not. The opened one was from Alder College, his safety, which wanted a deposit by the first of May. The sealed one was from Wexford, his first choice, which had put him on its waitlist in March and had said nothing since.

"Have you touched it?" Ms. Doyle asked, nodding at the sealed envelope, though it was obviously a letter about housing forms for the safety school and not, as Evan had briefly hoped when he'd seen the return address, a secret early promotion off the waitlist.

"I know what's in it," Evan said. "It's dorm stuff. For a school I don't want to go to."

Ms. Doyle folded her hands, which was her way of saying take your time, and Evan took it. He thought about his father, who worked in insurance and believed in backup plans the way other men believed in God, and about his mother, who had said only, "You waited four years to hear from them. You can wait a little longer." Two positions, cleanly opposed. He had been carrying both around for a week like luggage he refused to set down.

His phone buzzed against his thigh. Heather, from his stats class, who was waitlisted at her own first choice in Ohio: "Did you know waitlist spots mostly fill in May? Like after May 1. After everyone's deposits are in and the college knows how many places are actually open." He read it twice. So the deposit deadline at Alder and the waitlist movement at Wexford were not a race between them; the deposit came first, always, and the waitlist followed. The two letters on the desk were not enemies. They were a sequence.

"Good news or bad news?" Ms. Doyle said, watching his face.

"Weird news," Evan said, and turned the phone so she could read it. "Heather figured out the timing. Waitlists fill in May, after deposits are due. So if I put the deposit down at Alder, I'm not giving up on Wexford. I'm buying the ticket while I wait for the upgrade."

"Which costs six hundred dollars," Ms. Doyle said, laconic, "for a seat you might not sit in."

"That's my dad's whole argument, in fewer words."

"Your dad sounds efficient."

Evan laughed, and the wobbly chair squeaked its approval. He tried to internalize the logic rather than just recite it, to feel it in his chest instead of holding it in his mouth like a coin: pay now, wait after, lose six hundred dollars or lose the whole year. It was arithmetic dressed up as a moral dilemma, and seeing that made him almost embarrassed for the week he'd spent treating it like philosophy.

Almost. Because there was still the sealed envelope, and the strange grief of planning for a school he was hoping to abandon. Heather had texted again: "I'm paying mine today. If we both get off our lists in May, we're celebrating. If not, at least we have somewhere to sleep in September." That was a third position, he thought, not his father's caution or his mother's patience but something closer to a truce between them, a rapprochement he had reached by accident, through somebody else's Google search. He was honest enough with himself to admit he hadn't figured it out alone, and that the part of him still waiting for a miracle hadn't fully surrendered. The math said one thing. The sealed envelope on the desk, with its cheerful stock photo of a residence hall, said something quieter.

He picked up his phone and opened the payment site for Alder College. The form asked, in cheerful gray text, whether he was excited to join the class of 2030. He typed his father's credit card number from memory, since he had already asked permission twice this week, and pressed submit, and the little wheel spun.

"Done," he said, and turned the phone face down on the desk.

Ms. Doyle slid the sealed envelope toward him with two fingers. "You still have to fill out the housing form," she said. "Even prophets need a place to live."

Evan picked it up and tore it open, and a laminated map of the Alder campus slid out and drifted to the floor, landing face up, showing him a quad he did not yet know and might never see.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
story:
Grace had the two articles side by side on the library table like patients waiting for a diagnosis, and she was getting nowhere with either of them. Both asked the same question, whether later school start times improved attendance, and both claimed to answer it, and somewhere between them, apparently, she was supposed to locate her own opinion. Mr. Ngo had been clear about that part. "A review is not a summary," he'd said on Tuesday, tapping the assignment sheet. "It's a judgment. You put the two pieces of evidence on the scale and you tell me which way it tips, and why." Grace had nodded then, the way one nods at a doctor saying it will only pinch, and now, three days before the draft was due, she was discovering the pinch.

The trouble was that the numbers seemed to disagree. The first study, a district survey, reported a p-value of 0.05 and called its result significant. The second, a smaller one, reported 0.19 and called its result suggestive. Grace understood significance the way she understood currency in a country she'd never visited: she knew it mattered, and she knew she was probably being overcharged.

Katarina dropped into the chair across from her with a granola bar and no ceremony. "You look like you're convalescing," she said. "From what?"

"From statistics." Grace turned the laptop so Katarina could see. "First article. It says the attendance effect was significant, p equals 0.05. So that one's solid, right?"

"Extremely solid," said Katarina, through granola. "Ninety-five percent."

"Ninety-five percent of what?"

Katarina stopped chewing, which for her was a form of alarm. "Of being right. That's what it means. Five percent chance it's wrong, ninety-five percent it's right. My brother says that about everything."

Grace wrote it down, because it sounded like the kind of thing that would be useful, and then looked at it and did not feel it become useful. Ninety-five percent likely to be right. She turned it over the way one turns over a stone to see whether anything lives under it. "But right about what? The whole hypothesis? That seems like a lot to get out of one number."

Abram arrived at the table mid-thought, as usual, already reading over her shoulder before his backpack hit the floor. "Reading about start times again? That's a truism at this point. Teenagers are tired. School starts early. Nobody needed a study."

"Then why did they do one?"

"Because we need to know whether moving the start time actually fixes attendance, or whether it's just something administrators do so they can say they did something."

Grace pulled up the methods section of the first article and read it slowly, twice, which was one more time than she'd read anything that week. The sentence was buried in a paragraph about hypothesis testing, and it used the phrase "under the null hypothesis," which she had to look up, and then look up again. When she sat back, something in her chest had rearranged itself slightly, the way furniture rearranges when you finally accept that the desk faces the wrong direction.

"Oh," she said.

"Oh, what?" said Katarina.

"It's not ninety-five percent likely to be right." Grace pointed at the sentence on the screen. "It's the other thing. A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as the ones they got, if there were truly no effect. That's what it says. So point-oh-five means: if changing the start time did nothing, there's a five percent chance you'd still see an attendance improvement this big. It's about the data, not about the hypothesis. It's not the probability that the hypothesis is true."

There was a pause in which Katarina finished her granola bar and Abram read the sentence for himself.

"Wait," Katarina said. "So the study isn't ninety-five percent right?"

"It might be right. It might not. The number doesn't say." Grace was almost laughing, though at what she wasn't sure. "Your brother owes a lot of people their money back."

Abram was already scanning the second article, the one with p equals 0.19. "So this one is saying, if there were no effect, there's a nineteen percent chance of seeing results this extreme. Which is, what, too easy to stumble into by accident. So they can't rule out the accident."

"Right. So the second study isn't wrong, exactly. It's just quieter about what it can rule out."

The scale she was supposed to build for Mr. Ngo suddenly looked different, and less like a scale. It wasn't that the first study was the good one and the second the weak one, a five and a nineteen sorted into right and wrong. The first study could rule out accident more confidently; the second couldn't. That was all the numbers said. The rest, whether the effect was real, whether the district should act, was a judgment she'd have to make with the numbers merely standing nearby, offering less than she'd initially paid them for.

She started a new paragraph. She wrote that the first study's evidence was stronger, then crossed out "stronger" because it wasn't quite the word, and wrote instead that the first study ruled out chance more confidently, and that this was not the same as proving the hypothesis true. She wrote that the second study's result was consistent with a real but smaller effect. She wrote, and then deleted, and then wrote again, that the question of what the district should do remained open on the evidence available.

Mr. Ngo caught her in the hallway on Monday, before she'd even handed anything in. "How's the review?"

"Harder than it looks," she said. "The first article has better numbers but the numbers mean less than they sound like they mean."

He considered that for a moment. "That's a good sentence," he said. "Put it in."

"Which part?"

"All of it," he said, and walked on toward the science wing, leaving her standing by the trophy case with her draft in her bag and the whole question still not settled, which, she was beginning to suspect, was the point. She took out her pen and added one line at the bottom of the page: I am still uncertain whether the effect is real, and I think the honest position is that both studies leave that open. Then she read it over, and left it in.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
Brendon had been playing the interviewer for three blocks, and he was getting worse at it, not better. "So, Carter," he said, hunching over the backpack he'd propped on his knees like a desk, "tell me why you want to work at Flannigan's Garden Center, and don't say money, because everybody says money and it makes my soul die a little."

"Fine," Carter said. "I want to emancipate myself from asking my mother for twenty dollars every time I need gas. I want to learn about plants. I want to be outside instead of in a basement playing games with you two."

"That last part I actually believe," said Ryker, from across the aisle. "The rest sounded like a hostage reading a statement."

The bus lurched around the corner by the water tower, and the backpack slid off Brendon's knees and into the aisle, taking Carter's practice resumé with it. Three copies, because Ms. Kaur had said always bring three, though she had not explained who the other two copies were for, and Carter had been too embarrassed to ask. He gathered them up while the eighth graders in the back laughed at nothing, which was their permanent condition.

"Your eyes," Brendon said, when they were reassembled. "You keep looking at my forehead. It's creepy. Look at my actual eyes."

"I'm blinking, Brendon. Humans blink."

"Not that much. You're blinking like a man confessing to a crime." Brendon leaned forward, elbows on knees, chin on fists, suddenly serious in the way he could be serious about ridiculous things. "Try it again. And this time answer the hard one. A customer says the tomatoes you sold her died. What do you do?"

Carter looked at his eyes, which was worse than looking at his forehead, because Brendon's eyes were ridiculous too, brown and enormous, and Carter had never once considered them before in his life. "I'd ask her how she planted them," he said. "Drainage, sun, watering. Then I'd replace them if it was our fault, and if it wasn't, I'd still show her the hardier varieties, because she's coming back either way and I'd rather she came back happy."

There was a pause. "That was actually trenchant," Ryker said, sounding betrayed. "When did you become competent?"

"I've been competent. You just weren't interviewing me." But Carter noticed something odd, which was that Brendon had leaned forward, and that he himself, without deciding to, had leaned forward too, the two of them angled toward each other like parentheses. He sat back. "Wait. Hold on. Why do I suddenly like you more when we're both hunched over?"

"Oh, that's a real thing," Ryker said. He was the person to ask, because his cousin had taken a psychology class at the community college and Ryker repeated its contents like scripture. "In 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements. It's not even conscious. You just like people who move like you."

"So it's a trick," Carter said.

"It's a finding," Ryker said, with dignity. "Tricks are when demagogues do it. Remember eighth grade, when Tyler got the whole grade to vote for him for treasurer by copying everyone's handshake? That was a trick. This is science."

The distinction did not feel as sturdy as Ryker made it sound, and Carter turned it over for the rest of the ride, watching the strip mall slide past. If he matched the interviewer's lean, and the interviewer liked him more, was the liking real? Or had he just manufactured a version of it, like doping for charm? He could see both sides and could not get them to agree, which was annoying, because he liked problems that ended. His father had a saying about that, something about the difference between questions and furniture, but Carter had stopped listening to the saying itself and only remembered the shape of it.

The interview was Saturday morning. Ms. Kaur turned out to be the manager on duty, which nobody had warned him about, and for one bad second he considered bolting back to the petunias. She had taught him sophomore English and had once written "see me" on an essay of his in red ink that he still thought about at odd hours. But she just pointed at the chair across the little folding table and said, "Three resumés. Interesting. Sit."

She asked about his schedule, then about a time he'd handled a difficult person, and he told the tomato story with Brendon's imaginary customer promoted to a real one, which felt less like lying than like rehearsal finally being put to use. Then she stopped taking notes and leaned back, arms crossed, and studied him.

He saw it happen, the exact moment, and his whole body wanted to lean back with her, mirror her, be liked. Instead he stayed where he was and said, "I read that people like you more when you copy their posture. So I'm deciding not to. If you like me, I want it to be on purpose."

Ms. Kaur looked at him for a long moment. Then she uncrossed her arms, leaned forward over the table, and said, "Eleven dollars an hour. Saturdays and Sundays. And Monday, you're going to tell me who Brendon is, because you said his name twice."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US Telecommunications Act of 1996 eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership, and the number of station owners then fell sharply even as the number of stations grew.
story:
The group chat had been named Senior Spring by Clayton, back when everything still felt temporary and nobody minded the cliché. Joseph opened it now in his aunt's kitchen in Columbus, where he'd come to look at the university, and typed: guys the radio here is playing the same morning show we have at home. Same host, same bits, same phone number for the traffic report. Kloe answered first, three minutes later, because she was still on her phone at midnight the way she always was. Same show how, she wrote. Like syndicated? No, Joseph typed. Same host saying he'll see you at the home opener. He wouldn't say that about a team four hundred miles away unless something was off.

Clayton, who liked to pontificate about anything involving money, took it from there. Obviously it's cheaper to pipe one voice into a hundred cities than to pay a hundred guys, he wrote, and Joseph could picture him leaning back, pleased with himself. Fine, Joseph replied, but who owns the pipes? He was genuinely asking. It had never occurred to him to wonder who was behind a voice on a dial, and now that he'd noticed the strangeness he couldn't put it down, the way a word repeated too often starts to look misspelled.

The next morning he asked his aunt, who ran the kitchen radio through her whole routine, and she said the station had been bought a few years back and the local afternoon guy was let go. She missed him, she said. He did the high school scores. Nobody did the scores now. Joseph sat with his coffee and thought about that, about a whole city's scores going unannounced, and he texted Kloe a question he'd been carrying since midnight: do you think anyone decides what counts as news, or does it just happen?

Kloe didn't answer for a while, and when she did it was with a link. She had gone looking, because Kloe couldn't leave a question alone either. It was an article about the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which she summarized in her flat, careful way: it eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership. Joseph read it twice. He'd assumed there was some limit, some rule saying one company couldn't just own everything, and the idea that the rule had been removed, deliberately, in his own lifetime, made the whole dial feel different. He typed: so anyone could buy as many as they wanted after that.

And then Kloe sent the part that kept him up. She'd found the numbers, or at least the shape of them: after the cap went, the number of station owners fell sharply, even as the number of stations grew. More stations, fewer owners. Joseph lay on his aunt's pull-out couch and turned that over. More doors in the hallway, and almost all the keys on one ring. Was that bad? He didn't know yet. It was just strange, and the strangeness had a history, and the history was recent.

He drove home Tuesday and stopped at the station where Mr. Ricci worked, the local AM place that still did the farm report and the school board meetings. Joseph had interned there one fall, mostly rewiring things, and Mr. Ricci had let him sit in on the afternoon show. He found him in the booth with headphones around his neck and asked, a little awkwardly, whether it was true that one company could own hundreds of stations now. Mr. Ricci laughed, not unkindly. "True," he said. "You want to know why we're still here, ask the owner. He's stubborn and he's local." That was the whole speech. Then he asked Joseph if he'd come back and run the board on Saturdays, since the last kid went off to college.

That night Clayton and Kloe got into it in the chat, the way they did. Clayton argued that consolidation was just efficiency, that a big company could fund better journalism than some scrappy local outfit with a transmitter and a prayer. Kloe pushed back: a company owned by people with interests, she wrote, and those interests don't check themselves at the studio door. Joseph watched the messages stack up and found himself refusing to pick a side, or rather picking both, partly. Scale could buy things, he typed, and it could also smooth things over, and the question was who was doing the smoothing and toward what. Clayton called that a cop-out. Maybe, Joseph wrote. I'd rather have a cop-out I can test than a theory I can't.

He had been thinking, all afternoon, about testimony. His mother's law firm had him file transcripts over the summer, depositions mostly, and he'd learned that the whole trick was noticing who benefited from which version of events. News felt like that to him now, a stack of depositions, and the useful question wasn't who's lying but who's paying for the transcript. He didn't type that part. Some thoughts were for the walk home, and the walk was good, cold enough that the radio towers on the ridge stood out bare against the last light, a dozen of them, blinking in no particular order, each one aimed at someone.

On Thursday the chat lit up again. Kloe had made a playlist of unsigned local bands, autochthonous stuff as she called it, music that could only have come up from this particular ground, and she'd sent it to the college radio station with a note asking if they'd play it. They wrote back within an hour. Sure, send more. Joseph read that and felt something in him tip, not toward a conclusion but toward a plan. He asked Mr. Ricci about Saturdays again, and about whether a high school score segment could be revived, and Mr. Ricci said bring your own coffee. The board was old, the mics were older, and the tower out back was rusting where it met the earth, but the signal still reached the whole county. Joseph texted the chat one line: first show is Saturday, two to six. Come by if you're home. Kloe replied with the playlist link and three exclamation points. Clayton replied, "I'll listen on the app, obviously."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: At the same interest rate, a longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.
story:
The used Corolla sat in the dealership lot for three days before Eli admitted he wanted it, and one more day before he told anyone. He told Brendan at lunch, and Brendan said what everyone said, which was that a car was freedom, though Brendan took the bus everywhere and had never once driven alone at midnight with the windows down just to see where the road went. The salesperson had offered him a payment of two hundred and thirty a month, and Eli had nearly shaken on it before asking for a night to think. His mother said talk to the credit union first. She said it while washing dishes, without turning around, which was how she said most important things.

The credit union on Marsh Street smelled like carpet and toner, and the loan officer had a plastic nameplate he kept glancing at as though it belonged to someone else. Ms. De Vries was at the next desk, helping an older member with a certificate, and Eli could hear her say the word "compounding" in a low, patient voice, the way you might say a name you were fond of. When his turn came he slid the dealership's paper across the desk. The loan officer looked at it and then at him and then back at the paper.

"Seven years," the man said. "That's how they got the payment down to two thirty." He turned the sheet toward Eli and tapped a figure near the bottom, a number larger than any Eli had ever been responsible for. "Same rate, but stretched out that long, you pay a lot more interest over the life of the loan. The monthly payment's lower. The total isn't."

Eli looked at the number. It was not that he hadn't known interest existed; it was that he had thought of it as a kind of weather, something that happened to money passively, and here it was laid out in rows like a bill for services he hadn't remembered ordering. The loan officer sketched two columns on a scrap of paper, five years and seven years, the same rate on both. The shorter term came with a monthly payment forty dollars higher. The longer term came with total interest more than a thousand dollars higher. Eli copied both columns onto his own hand, because the paper felt like it belonged to the bank and his hand belonged to him.

"If you take the shorter one," the loan officer said, "can you cover the payment and still put something away? Even fifty a month into savings here, the interest works for you instead of against you. It adds up the same way, just in your direction."

Outside, on the bench by the bike rack, Eli called Kacey, who was doing a summer research thing at the university and answered with the authority of someone who had been enrolled somewhere for six entire weeks. Kacey launched into something about how the whole credit system was designed to make long-term costs invisible, then apologized for being tangential, and Eli said no, keep going, but Kacey had already moved on to a rant about a seminar on existentialism where the professor apparently believed in nothing except attendance. "Everything is a choice you're accountable for," Kacey said, "and no one will make it for you, which is the terrifying part." Eli said he was deciding between two numbers. Kacey said numbers were exactly the kind of thing you were accountable for.

His mother picked him up at five. In the car he laid the scrap paper against the dashboard, the two columns in his own handwriting, and told her the whole thing: the lower payment, the higher total, the savings account with the interest that grew in his favor instead of the lender's. She listened the way she cooked, without hurrying. When he finished she said, "You know Brendan's cousin financed a truck over eight years and by the end he'd paid for it twice." Then, at the red light, she added, "It's your money. I mean that literally. Your paycheck."

Eli thought about that on the drive home, the paycheck from the garden center that had seemed so enormous in June and so ordinary by August. He understood now that the seven-year loan wasn't a scam exactly; the lower payment was real, and for someone whose month was genuinely tight, real mattered. It was a trade, not a trick. What he couldn't settle was whether he was that someone, whether forty dollars a month was a hardship or a habit, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't know yet, that the answer would only appear in the living of it. He did know he didn't want to still be paying for a Corolla in the year he graduated college, though, and he did know that the version of himself who watched a savings account creep upward was a person he'd like to meet.

Monday morning he took the bus to the dealership with the folded paper in his pocket, and when the salesperson smiled and said they could probably get him comfortable, Eli set the paper on the desk, pointed to the five-year column, and said, "This one, and I'd like to hear about the total, not the monthly."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Ontario requires most private residential landlords to use a government standard lease form for new leases, and a tenant can request one in writing if it was not provided.
story:
Nathaniel had spread both leases across the meat counter at the back of Mr. Leung's grocery store, where he worked Sundays sweeping and restocking, because it was the only flat surface big enough and Mr. Leung had told him he could, so long as he kept the work apron on and answered if a customer needed the deli scale. One lease was for a basement room near Kelvin's cousin's place; the other was for a shared two-bedroom with Alistair, six stops east on the bus. Both began September first. He had until Friday to tell them both yes or no.

The basement lease ran to four pages of dense type, and the landlord had written in extras: the tenant pays all utilities, the tenant covers snow removal, the tenant is responsible for any appliance repair under two hundred dollars. The two-bedroom lease was a printed form with a small government logo at the top, and it said the landlord paid for water while the tenants split hydro and gas. Nathaniel made a column for each and began adding, moving between the numbers and the freezer aisle whenever the bell at the deli rang.

Kelvin came in at noon for energy drinks and leaned over the counter, reading upside down. "The basement one's cheaper rent."

"Rent, maybe." Nathaniel turned the page around for him. "But look. Utilities aren't estimated in this one at all. And I'd be paying to fix his stove." He tapped the other lease. "This one's on the standard lease form. That government one."

"What's that?"

"It's the form Ontario makes landlords use. Most private landlords have to use it for new leases." He had found it the night before, scrolling at the kitchen table while his mother dried dishes behind him, and had read the line three times before he let himself believe it. "And if they don't give you one, you can ask for it in writing."

Kelvin peeled the tab off a can. "So the basement guy just printed whatever he wanted?"

"That's what it looks like."

The question had begun to metastasize the moment Nathaniel understood it: not whether the basement room was cheap, but why a landlord would avoid a form that was required. He thought of his mother, years ago, signing a lease for their old apartment above the laundromat, a lease that later turned out to promise things the landlord had never intended to honour. She had said only, when he asked about it last month, that she'd been tired and the rent had been low. He had always taken that as a kind of bromide, the thing adults say so they can stop talking about it. Standing at the meat counter now, adding hydro estimates in pencil, he wondered whether she had simply done the same arithmetic he was doing and accepted the risk because the risk was cheaper than the alternative.

Alistair arrived at two, smelling of the bus, and dropped his knapsack on a crate of oranges. "Tell me it's us. My dad already measured the hallway for my desk."

"Sit down and add this with me." Nathaniel slid the papers over. "Basement, eight-fifty plus utilities, which I can't even guess at because he didn't write estimates. Two-bedroom, eleven hundred split two ways, so five-fifty each, plus half of hydro and gas, which last winter averaged about ninety a month each according to the guy renting it."

Alistair did the subtraction twice. "So we're actually cheaper."

"Maybe. If his numbers are real." Nathaniel pulled the basement lease back. "But there's this. The two-bedroom's on the standard form. The basement one isn't. And if it wasn't provided, I can request one in writing. If the guy has to redo it on the proper form, some of those clauses might not survive."

"So ask."

"If I ask and he's the type to take it badly, I lose the room before I know the utilities. If I don't ask and sign anyway, I'm agreeing to fix his appliances." He looked down at his columns, at the pencilled totals, one solid and one full of guessing. He was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't know which risk was worse. He could request the form and watch the deal sour, or he could walk toward the thing he could actually count.

Mr. Leung came through with a carton of eggs, paused, and looked at the papers fanned across his counter. He didn't lecture. He only said, "When I signed for this store, I read every page twice and still missed things. You'll miss things too. Choose which things."

Nathaniel capped his pen. He took his phone from the apron pocket, opened a blank message to the basement landlord, and typed: I'm interested in the room, and I'd like to request the standard lease form in writing. His thumb hovered over send while the freezer case hummed behind him and Alistair watched without saying anything.

"Five seconds," Alistair said. "Then I'm measuring the hallway."

Nathaniel pressed send, and the swoosh of it going was louder than he expected in the quiet of the store.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: A blood pressure reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury: systolic pressure when the heart beats, over diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
story:
Zachary would tell you he studied for maybe an hour, which was true only if you counted the flashcards he never opened. What he actually did was stand in Grandpa's bathroom on Sunday afternoons, reading the instruction card taped beside the cuff, because Grandpa refused to measure himself and refused to throw the machine out.

The bathroom smelled of eucalyptus and rust. The cuff sat on the sink counter next to the denture cup, a beige box with a screen the size of a playing card. Grandpa sat on the closed toilet lid with his sleeve rolled up, forearms like knotted rope, and waited, because waiting was something he was good at and Zachary was not.

The first time, the numbers came up and Zachary read them aloud as if he'd known all along. "One thirty-eight over eighty-five." Rebeka had texted him the week before, from her aunt's pharmacy, where she'd tried the free machine by the door and photographed her result. She'd written, top number, bottom number, no idea, and Zachary had said he knew, which at the time was a lie he intended to make true.
