He'd looked it up that night, and later explained it to Grandpa, whose questions were slow and exact. "So the top one is the systolic," Zachary said, "that's the pressure in millimeters of mercury when the heart beats. The bottom is diastolic, when the heart relaxes between beats. That's all a reading is. Two numbers, beating and resting." Grandpa nodded the way he nodded at weather reports, as though filing it somewhere permanent.

What Zachary could not say was which numbers were good, exactly, or where the line lived between watch it and worry. The pamphlet from the clinic said diet and exercise change a reading over time, that the numbers move, and he'd told Grandpa this with a confidence he did not feel, the kind of confidence Grandpa's generation tried to inculcate in boys like it was a vaccination. Grandpa had been sanguine about the whole business. "Your grandmother's numbers were high for thirty years," he said, "and she outlived her doctor." Zachary wrote that down, later, in the notebook where he kept things he suspected were both true and useless.

He kept coming back, though, and that was the part he didn't examine. Sundays became Tuesdays too, then whenever Grandpa's voice on the phone sounded thin. He learned to seat the cuff two fingers above the elbow, to keep Grandpa's arm still and level with his heart, to wait out the squeeze of the pump with a joke about the machine trying to eat him.

In the notebook, he'd started a small grid. Dates down the side, numbers across. He liked the grid. It made the thing feel like arithmetic instead of waiting, and waiting, he'd begun to understand, was what his mother was doing in the kitchen downstairs every Sunday while he stood in the bathroom with a man neither of them would say out loud was getting smaller.

It was Rebeka who caught the flaw, one afternoon when she came by with the flashcards after all. She stood in the bathroom doorway while Zachary ran the cuff, watching him ease Grandpa's arm in. "You do it left-handed on yourself," she said. He told her he didn't. She picked up the notebook, flipped to the first page, and turned it toward him. The earliest entry wasn't Grandpa's name at the top of the grid. It said Z, in his own handwriting, dated the week before he'd ever brought Grandpa in here, the week after the phone call from his mother about tests, the week he'd wanted to practice on someone whose numbers he could afford to see. He took the notebook back and closed it, and Grandpa, sleeve still rolled, held out his arm. "Today," Grandpa said, "I want the bottom one."

"Diastolic," Zachary said, and wrapped the cuff.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand.
story:
Sarah had the thermometer clipped to the side of the pot like it might betray her if she looked away. The chocolate had reached 45 degrees and now it had to come down, and every recipe she'd read disagreed about how: some said pour it onto marble, some said seed it with chopped chocolate, all of them spoke in the assured tone of people who had never burned a batch on a Tuesday afternoon while their mother asked from the hallway whether the kitchen was supposed to smell like that.

She stirred. The evening before, at the farmers' market, Nicola had held one of the small dark squares from the confectioner's table against her palm, waiting for it to soften, and it hadn't. She'd put it in her mouth and it had gone liquid almost at once, and she'd demanded an explanation with the indignation of someone being tricked. Sarah had said she didn't know. Then she'd gone home and looked it up, and the answer had felt like being handed a key to a room she'd walked past for years.

Form V, the website had called it, the desirable crystal form, and the number had stuck in her head. She said it aloud now, partly to steady herself. "Thirty-three point eight."

"Is that a temperature or a curse," said Corinne, who was sitting on the counter with her ankles crossed, eating the failed batch of yesterday, the one that had set dull and streaked and bent instead of snapping. Corinne had announced on arrival that this whole project was a waste of a Saturday, that chocolate was chocolate, that Sarah's obsession with doing things the hard way was, in her word, cerebral, and that she herself was only here for the leftovers.

"It's the temperature," Sarah said. "Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius. Just below body temperature." She tapped the thermometer. "That's why good chocolate melts in your mouth but not in your hand. Yesterday I got it too hot, so the wrong crystals formed and it set like candle wax."

"So it's a solid on the table and a liquid on your tongue because it melts at 33.8," Corinne said, "which is colder than you are but warmer than the table."

"That's it."

Corinne looked at the square she was eating, then at the grey-bloomed sheet of yesterday's failure still sitting on the counter beside her, and said nothing, which for Corinne was close to concession.

Sarah cooled the chocolate on the marble slab Mr. Yang had lent her. He was their neighbour from two floors down, a retired chemist who kept a slab of polished marble in his apartment for reasons she'd never learned and hadn't asked about, and when she'd knocked on his door that morning holding her pot he had looked at it, looked at her, and gone to get the stone without a single question. He'd only said, at the door, "Don't let it seize," which she'd had to look up too.

She spread the chocolate with the spatula, pulled it back, spread it again, watching the temperature edge down through the thirties. The room smelled sweet and faintly bitter at once. Her mother drifted through for a glass of water, paused, and said, "Careful, that looks like it could incapacitate you for a week if you burned yourself," and drifted out again. Sarah kept working. At 31 degrees she scraped it back into the pot and warmed it gently, nudge by nudge, toward 32.

From the doorway, Corinne watched her. She had assumed, coming over, that this was vanity, that Sarah wanted to post a picture of glossy truffles and feel superior. But Sarah wasn't taking pictures. She was bent over the thermometer with her lip between her teeth, adjusting the heat by degrees so small the numbers barely moved, treating a pot of melted chocolate like something that could be understood rather than merely eaten. Corinne thought about the market, about Nicola's square sitting solid in the heat of her hand, about the 33.8 that made it dissolve the instant it touched her tongue. There was something in that, she admitted to herself, something that made the world briefly legible. Maybe the hard way wasn't showing off. Maybe it was just a different way of tasting.

"I want to do the next one," Corinne said, hopping off the counter. "Move over."

"Your hands are warm."

"So are yours. Wash them in cold water first."

Sarah yielded the spatula and clipped the thermometer where Corinne could read it. Together they watched the number hold, and Sarah poured a test stripe onto parchment, thin and dark. They waited. In the quiet of the cooling kitchen it set with a sheen neither of them had managed before, a small, hard brightness.

Corinne took a corner and broke it, and it snapped.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homophily, a term from sociologists Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton in 1954, is the tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves.
story:
Cohen had counted the tables in the cafeteria before he'd counted anything else about Millbrook High. There were eleven, and by the second day he could see how they sorted themselves: the runners near the windows, the gamers in the corner with their laptops out, the theater kids in a loud ring by the door. He stood in the lunch line with his tray and understood that choosing a table was choosing a version of himself, and that he had no idea which version he wanted.

Back in his old town he had never had to choose. He and Alessio had been friends since kindergarten, the kind of friendship that had never once been negotiated. Since the move, Alessio sent messages that Cohen answered late, and then later, and he could feel the thread thinning in his hands. His father had said it would get easier. His father said a lot of things like that, in the patient voice of someone who had once been the new kid himself.

On Thursday, a boy from his history class sat down across from him at the empty end of a table. His name was Justus, and he had an opinion about everything, including the cafeteria. "Look at them," Justus said, gesturing with a plastic fork. "Every table thinks it's about personality, but it's not. It's about sameness. Runners sit with runners." He stabbed a piece of lasagna. "It's called homophily. Sociologists named it. Lazarsfeld and Merton, 1954. The tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves." He said it fast, like a fact he'd been waiting all week to spend on someone.

"Homo as in same," Cohen said. "Not the other thing."

"Just so." Justus looked pleased. "So the smart move is to figure out what you are and find your table."

Cohen thought about that for the rest of the day. It was a parsimonious theory, he had to admit, one clean idea explaining every table in the room. But it bothered him, and he couldn't say why until he was walking home past the strip mall and the shuttered video store his mother kept saying would become a bakery. What bothered him was that Alessio was nothing like him. Alessio was loud where Cohen was quiet, reckless where Cohen was careful, and for eleven years the difference had been the whole point.

On Friday he tested it. He sat with the gamers because he had, at his old school, been the kid who played strategy games on rainy lunches. Two of them nodded at him. One asked what he played. But the conversation kept snagging on the games he didn't know, the in-jokes from a year of sessions he hadn't attended, and by the time the bell rang he had said maybe forty words. Sameness, it turned out, was not a door you could just walk through. It was more like a wall with a small gate in it, and the gate had been built while he was living somewhere else.

He remonstrated with himself on the walk home, quietly, the way you argue with a map when the road has moved. He had taken Justus's fact and turned it into an instruction, and it had failed, and neither the fact nor the failure seemed entirely honest on its own. People did cluster by similarity. He could see it at every table. But the clustering took time, and it took shared history, and maybe what he'd had with Alessio was the exception that proved similarity wasn't the whole engine, or maybe it was just similarity of a kind nobody had measured yet.

On Monday, Justus found him before history and asked how the table experiment had gone. Cohen told him the truth: that the theory held up when you looked across the whole room, and fell apart the moment you tried to use it. Justus considered this with what looked like genuine interest. "So what are you going to do instead?"

"I don't know yet," Cohen said. "Sit somewhere until it's somewhere."

Justus laughed, a short bark that made a girl at the next locker turn around. "That's the least scientific plan I've ever heard."

That afternoon Cohen found Ms. Moose, the librarian, shelving returns in the quiet section, and asked if the library had anything by a sociologist named Lazarsfeld. She led him back to the stacks without asking why, which he appreciated, and slid a thick book into his hands. He carried it to a table by the window where a girl was already reading, her own stack beside her, three books deep, and he set his one book down across from her and opened it to the index.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The card on Nathaniel's station read, in Ms. Adebayo's looping hand, "Family dinner, mountain cabin, elevation 5,000 feet, one burner." He turned it over hoping for a hint on the back and found only a coffee ring, which he chose to read as a sign of Ms. Adebayo's long career rather than of anything about his grade.

"You got the cabin," Harry said, leaning over from the next station with the entitlement of someone who had already burned his onions. "I got 'weeknight, picky toddler.' I would trade you my firstborn for that cabin."

"Your firstborn is hypothetical," Arlo said without looking up from his knife. "You'd be trading nothing for something. That's not a trade, that's a scam."

Nathaniel spread his ingredients and felt the old frustration arrive before the memory did, the way sedimentary rock layers hold old weather: pressed down, but still there, in order. Last April, at his father's cabin above the tree line, he had stood over a single burner while his father unpacked boxes in the next room, boxes that were going to Denver, and the pasta had come out of the pot after eleven minutes exactly as the box promised, and it crunched. His father had eaten it anyway, chewing philosophically, and said the box was written for people who lived lower down. Nathaniel had blamed the stove, the pot, the brand, everything but the thin bright air itself, because blaming the air felt like blaming the place, and the place was the only thing about that weekend he wanted to keep.

Now Ms. Adebayo circled the room, and when she reached his station he asked, keeping his voice level, whether the pasta would take longer at the cabin.

"That's your problem to solve," she said, which was how she answered everything, and moved on to rescue Harry's onions.

The apportionment of class time was posted on the whiteboard, forty minutes for cooking, ten for plating, and Nathaniel watched the clock the way his father watched the road on long drives, with patience that was mostly pretend. He put the water on early, before he even opened the sauce, and Arlo noticed.

"Water first? You usually do sauce first. You're a sauce-first guy. You have a philosophy."

"Up there, water boils at a lower temperature," Nathaniel said. "About ninety-five degrees Celsius at five thousand feet. So anything boiled takes longer. The water takes longer to get going, the pasta takes longer after. My dad's cabin taught me that the expensive way."

"So how much longer?"

"I don't know exactly," Nathaniel admitted, and it cost him something to say it in a graded room. "I'm going to test it. Every minute past the box time, I pull one piece." He set five strands of spaghetti on a saucer like evidence.

He tasted at eleven minutes, twelve, thirteen. At thirteen and a half the strand bent against his teeth instead of snapping, and he salted the sauce and lowered the heat and thought about his father chewing that crunchy pasta with such ceremony, saying it built character, saying a lot of things that spring that were meant to extenuate the move and only made the distance more specific. The dinner Nathaniel was assembling here had a real destination: tonight he was cooking for his mother and his little brother, who ate like a small polite locust, and the assignment meal and the real meal had merged somewhere in his head without asking permission.

Harry drifted over holding his toddler card like a losing lottery ticket. "Mine just refuses beans on principle. Yours requires physics."

"It's not physics," Arlo called. "It's geography."

"It's both, probably," Nathaniel said, and drained the pasta, and the steam rose up between him and the whiteboard and blurred the schedule so that for a second the numbers were only weather.

At the end of class Ms. Adebayo tasted his pasta, held it a moment, and wrote something in her binder that he could not see. She looked at his saucer of test strands, laid out in their minute-by-minute sequence, and then at him. "You kept the evidence," she said. "Most students throw out their failures."

"They're not failures," Nathaniel said. "They're minutes."

He packed the meal into two containers, one for the grade and one for home, and Harry carried the door open for him with a bow. "Feed the locust," Harry said. "Tell him the cabin says hi."

"Tell it yourself," Nathaniel said. "It's my dad's cabin. Maybe at Christmas."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
The community art studio occupied the back half of a converted laundromat, and on Saturday afternoons it smelled of linseed oil and the instant noodles Ms. Haddad made in the back room. Tristan had claimed the corner table by the window because the light there was honest. On the easel in front of him was a half-primed board he intended, eventually, to become a painting of the harbor his grandmother talked about, the one she hadn't seen since before her surgery. She was convalescing at his aunt's house now, able to sit up, able to complain, which his mother said was a good sign, and Tristan had decided a painting would reach her faster than a phone call.

The problem was the water. His grandmother had described it as bright, almost aggressive, a green so sharp it hurt to look at on sunny days. Tristan had squeezed out viridian, then added yellow, then more yellow, then a slug of blue because the green had gone flat, then white because the whole thing had gone dark, and now his palette held the color of a puddle in a parking lot. He dipped the brush in and dragged a stripe of it across a scrap of board. It looked like something you would step over.

Lance wandered over from the printmaking table with ink on his knuckles. "That's supposed to be water?"

"It's a work in progress."

"It's the color of my uncle's couch." Lance picked up the scrap, considered it, and put it down with the exaggerated care of someone handling evidence. Behind him, the retired sign painter who came on Saturdays, a saturnine man who critiqued everyone's work in three words or fewer, glanced at the stripe and said only, "Mud."

Tristan scraped the puddle into the trash and started again. Fresh yellow, a careful touch of green, a thread of blue. Better, but still like water in a jar, not water at sea. He added more blue. The color sank. He added white. It went pale and chalky, then, when he pushed more green into it, gray. He was on his fourth attempt when Tea sat down across from him, opened her sketchbook, and watched him murder another mixture.

"You're doing it backwards," she said.

"Nobody asked."

"It's subtractive," Tea said. "Paint, I mean. Every pigment eats some of the light, so the more you pile in, the darker it gets. It goes toward brown, not toward white. It's not like mixing light." She turned her sketchbook around to show a page of small, clean squares, each one a single mixture of only two pigments, unmuddied.

Tristan looked at his palette, which now held six distinct shades of disappointment. "So the bright color I want doesn't exist in a pile."

"It exists in a thin one. Two pigments, maybe three. After that you're just subtracting." She tapped the brightest square on her page, a green mixed from yellow and a blue she'd labeled in pencil. "You could glaze it, too. Thin layers over dry ones."

He had wanted to mix his way there, the way he'd once spent an afternoon adding ingredients to a smoothie until it became undrinkable, believing the whole time that one more addition would fix it. There was a version of his grandmother's harbor that required restraint, not abundance, and he wasn't sure he liked that, because restraint felt like admitting the bright thing was partly made of the darker thing beneath it. But he wiped the palette nearly clean, laid out just the yellow and the blue, and mixed a small amount, no more than a shell of it. It was close. It was not the color in his grandmother's voice when she described the water, but it was a color that could stand in a painting next to others and hold its own.

Before he could start the underpainting, Tea cleared her throat. "You're using my cadmium. The tube with the tape on it."

He looked down. The tape was hers, and the tube was half its original weight. Earlier that week he had told the whole studio table that her landscape looked like a greeting card, which she had not answered, and which he had not apologized for, because the apology would have been worse than a silence, or so he had told himself. He got up, went to the supply shelf Ms. Haddad kept for the studio's shared stock, found an unopened yellow, and set it beside Tea's elbow.

"That's for the tube," he said. "The greeting card thing is a separate payment." She snorted, which was as close to absolution as the studio offered, and scored a line into her lino block with her thumb guarding the blade.

Tristan primed the panel with a thin, even layer of the dark mixture, the honest one, and set it by the window to dry, turning it once so the light crossed it flat.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US fairness doctrine, introduced in 1949, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues; the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987.
story:
The cursor blinked in the search box while Sierra's tea went cold beside the keyboard. She had typed and deleted three versions of the same question: who owns KRL News. The story she wanted to write for Ms. Tang's class was about the grain elevator fire two miles from school, the one the district had called "a contained incident" in a robocall while ash settled on the tennis courts. Taylor's asthma had kept her home for three days afterward. Nobody had explained why.

She typed it plain this time: KRL News ownership. The first result was a Wikipedia page for Hollen Media Group, and the second was a press release from four years ago announcing that Hollen had acquired KRL's parent company for an undisclosed sum. Sierra scrolled with two fingers, fast at first, then slower. Hollen Media Group also owned the grain terminal. The grain terminal that had burned.

Her grandfather called while she was still staring at the page, which was strange, because he only called on Sundays. "Your mother says you're investigating something," he said. She could hear the television behind him, low, the way he kept it all day. "A fire."

"A fire and maybe a cover-up," she said. "The only station covering it is owned by the same company that owned the building. And they keep saying the air quality tests came back fine."

There was a pause long enough that she checked whether the call had dropped. Then her grandfather laughed, a dry sound. "You know, when I was younger, they couldn't do that. The TV stations had to show both sides. It was called the fairness doctrine." He said it the way he said playoff scores, like a fact that had always been true and then wasn't.

"What happened to it?"

"Look it up. Your grandmother wants the kettle." He was gone before she could ask anything else, which was his way, and she sat with the phrase he'd left her, the fairness doctrine, turning it over the way you turn a key you found in a drawer.

The search took forty seconds. The FCC had introduced it in 1949, and it required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues. The same FCC abolished it in 1987, years before she was born. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, because it seemed to change shape as she read it. Her whole life, the rule had been gone. Hussein had argued in class last week that media bias was just something you developed an eye for, like weather, and she had agreed, and now she understood that there had once been an umbrella and somebody had taken it away, and the rain had simply become the sky.

She opened a new tab and messaged him. Hussein answered within a minute, which meant he was supposed to be studying. "So they had to give both sides," he typed. "Who decided what counted as controversial?" She didn't know. She typed that she didn't know, and it felt like the first honest sentence she'd written all night. The doctrine was gone and the questions it used to force were now voluntary, and voluntary questions were the first thing a recalcitrant accountant cut when the newsroom and the grain terminal shared a balance sheet.

That was the part she couldn't prove. She had a press release, a corporate family tree, and a robocall. She had Taylor's inhaler and a photograph she'd taken of the ash on the courts, gray and fine, already calcifying into a crust where the sprinklers had wet it. What she did not have was anything connecting the "fine" air quality result to the ownership, except the shape of the thing, the convenient geometry of it, and Ms. Tang had told them in September that a shape was not evidence. "A shape is where you start digging," she'd said. Sierra had written it in the margin of her notebook and underlined it twice.

She found the old broadcast anyway. A public television archive, grainy footage from 1984, a panel discussion about pesticide regulation: an industry man in a brown suit, then a farmer, then a scientist, given equal minutes in sequence, as if fairness were a matter of arithmetic. Sierra watched all eleven minutes even though the topic bored her, because the format itself did not bore her. Both sides, in the same room, unavoidable. She tried to imagine KRL airing a scientist alongside its own air quality report and heard, in her head, the silence where the segment would go.

At ten her mother knocked and stood in the doorway with a folded towel she didn't seem to need. "Your grandfather says you learned something about television."

"It's for the school paper. Ms. Tang's class." Sierra angled the screen without thinking about it, a small movement, and her mother noticed the movement, which was worse than anything on the screen. "The station that says the air is fine is owned by the company that owned the fire."

Her mother set the towel on the desk. "That's why he called me first," she said. "Your Uncle Denny works at the terminal. He's been on leave since it burned." Sierra felt the room reorganize itself around this. The leave, the cousins' birthday she'd missed in March, her mother's careful phone voice lately, all of it suddenly part of the same corporate family tree. "If you write this, it lands on him. They're offering recompense for the smoke days, he said. A settlement, if nobody makes noise."

Sierra looked at the archive tab, still open, the farmer mid-sentence with his hands out. She thought about fairness being arithmetic, about voluntary questions, about her uncle's mortgage and Taylor's lungs, and she did not know how to hold all of it in one article, or whether holding it was the same as resolving it. She pulled the keyboard toward her and opened a new document. She titled it with the date and the fire, and underneath she typed a single line: The air quality tests were commissioned by Hollen Media Group, which owns both the terminal and the station reporting the results.

She looked at the line for a long time. Then she picked up her phone and texted Taylor: "Can I come by tomorrow? Bring your inhaler records."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
Sydney had been standing outside the bookstore in the west wing of the mall for eleven minutes when Layton appeared beside the pretzel cart, wearing a collared shirt she had never seen him in, which made the whole evening feel suddenly formal and slightly absurd. They had biology together. He had asked her out on Tuesday, in the parking lot, holding his car keys like a man surrendering evidence. She had said yes partly because she wanted to and partly to prove to Camron that she was capable of saying yes to anything at all.

"Okay, ground rules," Layton said when he reached her. "I'm impecunious, so dinner is a wetzel and a shared lemonade, and I'm going to pretend that's charming."

"It is charming," Sydney said, and found that she meant it, which surprised her. He held up the pretzel like a trophy, and they walked.

The mall on a Friday night was its own ecosystem, loud and greasy and bright, seniors commanding the benches near the fountain as though the benches were thrones. Sydney had spent the walk from the bus rehearsing versions of herself: the easy one, the funny one, the one who let silences sit without rushing to fill them. Around Layton the rehearsal kept slipping, and what came out instead was something more crooked and more true.

They talked about the genetics unit first, which should have been boring but wasn't. Layton explained his project on fruit fly genotypes with his hands, drawing Punnett squares in the air, and Sydney laughed so hard at his impression of the vice principal reading the rubric that a woman at the next table looked over. Ms. Romano, it turned out, working the closing shift at the bookstore, stacking remainders by the café. She raised an eyebrow at the two of them, at the shared lemonade with two straws, and Sydney felt her face go hot, because of course a teacher would materialize on the one night it mattered.

"Gojii," Ms. Romano said as they passed, mispronouncing Sydney's name the way she had all semester, and then, getting it right: "Sydney. Don't stay past closing. Security gets territorial."

After that they wandered, and somewhere between the arcade and the exit doors, Layton reached over and took her hand. Sydney had been watching his hand move for half a corridor, so she had time to decide, and she let him. His palm was warm and a little damp and she thought, okay, this is fine, I wanted this, I chose this. They walked that way past the sunglasses kiosk, past a group of boys from the rival school who whooped at them, past the fountain where the seniors held court.

Then, somewhere near the escalator, the wanting stopped. It wasn't him. His thumb had started tracing a slow circle on the back of her hand, and the circle was fine, objectively fine, but her chest had gone tight in a way she recognized from exams and phone calls from her father, and her hand in his felt like a thing she was maintaining rather than a thing she was enjoying. She kept holding on for two more storefronts because she had said yes, because withdrawing felt like breaking a contract, because Camron would say she was being dramatic.

In health class in the spring they had spent a whole period on consent, and she had half-listened through it, doodling in the margin, until the teacher had said one sentence that snagged in her: consent can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given. Any time. Even after. She had written it in the margin without knowing why, and now, near the Sunglass Hut, the words came back with their full weight, and she understood that a yes given at the pretzel cart did not bind her at the escalator.

"Layton," she said. "Can we not, with the hand? I did want to. I don't really want to anymore."

He let go before she finished the sentence, so quickly that her hand felt colder than the air warranted. "Yeah, of course," he said. "You don't have to explain."

"I kind of want to anyway," Sydney said. "It's not you. I just learned that it's allowed, changing your mind halfway. It's allowed even after you said yes. I keep forgetting that's true for things besides hand-holding."

Layton nodded, and she watched him take it in, watched him not argue, watched him slide his hands into his pockets instead. They walked on with a foot of air between them, and the air was not cold. Outside the glass doors the parking lot was turning amber under the streetlights, and Camron was visible through the window of the arcade, losing at some racing game and enjoying it.

"Do you still want the rest of the pretzel?" Layton asked. "Because I'm telling you now, I will absolutely commandeer it if you don't claim it."

"Split it," Sydney said, and held out her hand for it, this time because she had decided to, all over again.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: An equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
story:
The summer before college, Sebastian's grandfather had started leaving the porch light on all night, and nobody in the family said why out loud. Sebastian noticed it the evening he arrived, suitcase thudding on the welcome mat, his grandmother's hands already reaching for it before he'd offered. He had brought his chemistry notebook because the placement exam was in nine days, and because he had nowhere else to be.

He studied at the kitchen table under the hum of the old fridge, working problem after problem about equilibrium. The words slid off him. Shift left, shift right, heat as a product or a reactant, and he could follow the recipe without feeling that he understood anything at all. His grandfather shuffled in at intervals for water, and the fourth time he stopped behind Sebastian's chair and read the page upside down for a long moment, saying nothing, which was his way of asking.

"It's Le Chatelier," Sebastian said finally, spinning the notebook halfway. "If you change the temperature, the reaction shifts to counteract the change. Raise the heat, and it goes whichever direction absorbs heat. Like the reaction is stubborn."

"Stubborn," his grandfather repeated, as if tasting it. He lowered himself into the opposite chair, slow, one hand flat on the table. "Come with me tomorrow. I want to show you the shop. I can't drive at night anymore."

Sebastian knew about the shop the way he knew about his grandfather's war stories, which was to say indirectly, through overheard arguments between his mother and her sister about whether the place should be sold. He said yes, and in the morning he found himself behind the counter of a hardware store that smelled of seed packets and machine oil, watching his grandfather greet customers by name while Tessa's texts stacked up on his phone. She and Khadija were at the lake. He typed soon, maybe tomorrow, and put the phone in his pocket.

The afternoon did something to the store that Sebastian couldn't name at first. People came and went constantly, but the crowd inside stayed the same size, maybe a dozen, all afternoon. Two would leave as two more pushed through the door, and when a school group swelled the aisles at three o'clock, the flow out through the registers quickened until the room settled again. His grandfather rang up purchases with an arithmetic that seemed almost chemical, opening a second lane or closing it, coaxing the store back to its steady dozen.

"That's it," Sebastian said, quieter than he meant to. He was restocking a shelf of washers, and the feeling arrived like a door unlocking. "Equilibrium. Forward and reverse reactions, both still happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant even though nothing stops." He looked at his grandfather. "People are leaving and entering at the same speed. The shop never fills up."

His grandfather smiled at the register rather than at Sebastian. "Everything in this store is moving," he said. "Nothing is still."

Sebastian thought about that on the drive back, the fields going amber, the igneous paperweight on the dashboard absorbing the sun so that it was warm to touch even after the shade returned. In the liminality of that last week before everything changed, between his grandfather's dwindling daylight and his own unread future, he sat at the kitchen table again and this time the problems behaved. Heat the reaction and it shifted, cooling it and it shifted back, the system absorbing the blow like the shop absorbing the school group. What he still couldn't decide was whether the principle was a description or a comfort, whether systems really resisted change or merely revealed what they had been all along. He wrote his uncertainty in the margin, small, in pencil.

On his last night, he called Tessa from the porch, and while she talked about the lake and Khadija's terrible sunscreen application, he noticed the porch light burning against the dark. It stayed on now for a reason nobody would say, and his grandmother had stopped turning it off, and tomorrow he would drive away and the house would keep doing what it did, forward and reverse, the same number of people inside, everything moving, nothing still. Before bed he checked that the outside steps were clear of the garden hose, coiling it back against the wall where his grandfather wouldn't trip in the morning light.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Raphael had ironed the shirt twice, and it still looked like something that had been ironed in a panic, which it had. He stood in the hallway holding his phone, thumb hovering over the message he had drafted to Seamus. "Can't do dinner tonight," it read, "something came up." Nothing had come up. Nothing was going to come up. He deleted it one letter at a time, as though slow deletion were more honest than fast.

The date was with a girl from his philosophy elective, the one who had argued, in the second week of term, that altruism was just selfishness wearing a nice coat. Raphael had disagreed in front of everyone, at length, with more heat than the point deserved, and afterward she had said, "You argue like you're afraid of being wrong," and he had thought about that sentence roughly every day since. When she asked him out, three weeks later, he assumed it was a setup for another debate. It was not. It was a date, at a small restaurant near the canal, seven o'clock.

"You're doing the thing," Alejandro said from the couch, where he had spread his chemistry notes like a man building a nest. "The replay thing. You're staring at the middle distance and composing your own obituary."

"I'm deciding what shirt to wear."

"You're wearing the shirt. You're deciding whether to go." Alejandro had known him since they were eleven, which meant he had archival footage of every version of Raphael, including the one who, in grade nine, had called a substitute teacher's jokes "a bit acerbic" and been mocked for a week. "Here's my position," Alejandro went on, folding his hands like a professor. "You go, you're awkward for forty minutes, you come home, it's over. You cancel, you're awkward forever."

"That's a false binary."

"It's a true binary. Go put on shoes."

At the restaurant she was already there, sitting with her coat still on, which Raphael decided meant she was about to leave. She took the coat off when she saw him. She ordered the mussels because, she said, she liked food that required strategy, and he spent the first ten minutes cataloguing everything he said for errors, the way he used to proofread essays by reading them backwards. At one point he used the word "dysphemism" to describe how his grandfather called all vegetables "rabbit food," and he heard himself and thought, who talks like that, and she laughed, actually laughed, and asked whether his grandfather had terms for other food groups.

By dessert the cataloguing had slowed. She told him about her brother, who had taught himself to juggle during a broken leg and now juggled at parties uninvited, and Raphael told her about Seamus, who had a habit of narrating ordinary actions in the third person ("Seamus waits for the bus. Seamus grows impatient"). She said that people who narrate themselves are just people trying to see how they look from outside, and he said that was probably everyone, and she said, "Then it's strange that we're all so bad at it," and he felt the sentence settle somewhere and stay.

They stood outside the restaurant afterward in the cold, and the goodbye had a small misfire in it, a hug that became a wave halfway through, and he walked home composing the autopsy. It had been a disaster. The mussel strategy had taken too long. The dysphemism thing. The moment he'd talked over her story about Portugal. By the time he reached his street he had built the whole case and convicted himself.

At home his father was awake, reading at the kitchen table, and behind him on the counter, spine out, was a library book Raphael had brought home last week and not opened: a collection of psychology writing for a personal essay he was supposed to be drafting for Mr. Aydın's class. He poured himself water and, avoiding his father's questions with a shrug and a grin, flipped it open at random while the kettle worked.

There it was, a paragraph about a 2018 study by Erica Boothby and her colleagues, who had found something they called the liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. Raphael read it twice. He thought of the hug-becoming-wave. He thought of her asking, twice, questions about things he had mentioned only in passing, which was not, he realized, a thing you did to someone whose company you were enduring.

He caught himself doing it anyway, the autopsy, the backwards proofreading, because knowing about the gap was not the same as closing it. Maybe she had liked him and maybe she had liked the mussels and been neutral about him, and no study of strangers' first conversations could settle what had happened between two specific people at a canal-side table. He could hold both: the evidence that his own judgment of the evening was probably rigged against him, and the honest admission that he could not know hers. He picked up his phone and typed, "I had a good time. Grandfather also calls oatmeal 'wallpaper paste,' if you wanted the full glossary," and then he sat with his thumb over send, and his father looked up from his book, and Raphael pressed it.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The 2018 Gender Shades study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru found commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women but under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men.
story:
The group project was due on Friday, and Anthony had volunteered to assemble the photo essay because he was the only one with a laptop that didn't stall on video files. He sat at his desk with a mug of tea going cold beside the trackpad, dragging folders of images from a shared drive. The class had gone on a field trip to the montane research station above the valley, where the air thinned and the pines gave way to wind-stunted spruce, and Ms. Lim had assigned each of them a theme. Kelly-Ann's theme was geology; Adrien's was lichen. Anthony's was light.

The photo software was supposed to make the assembly quick. It tagged faces automatically, grouped shots by person, offered little collages. He imported the first batch and watched the thumbnails populate with neat grey labels. Adrien's face appeared in the sidebar within seconds, recognized again and again: Adrien on the ridge, Adrien at the seismograph, Adrien laughing with his hood up. Every picture of Kelly-Ann came back blank. Not mislabeled. Blank, as though the frame contained rocks and weather and no one at all.

He assumed it was the lighting. He had read enough forum posts to blame lighting for everything. But the pattern held through two hundred photographs: the overcast shots, the bright ones, the ones where she stood beside Adrien in identical conditions. The software found Adrien and lost Kelly-Ann every single time. He tried cropping her face larger. He tried sharpening. In one photo she stood directly in front of the station's white wall at noon, and still the box around her face stayed empty.

He typed the problem into the search bar, hesitated, then typed it more honestly: why doesn't facial recognition work on darker skin. The results came back fast. He read for an hour, tea long cold, while his mother passed the doorway twice with laundry and he barely registered her. There was a study from 2018, called Gender Shades, by two researchers whose names he said aloud to fix them in memory, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru. They had tested commercial facial analysis systems and found error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women, and under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men. He read the numbers twice, then a third time. Under one percent. Thirty-four point seven. The gap wasn't a rounding error; it was the width of the entire world Kelly-Ann lived in.

He thought about the school's new entry system, the cameras above the gym doors that were supposed to log tardy students automatically. He thought about who got flagged and who walked through. He had never had to think about it, which was, he understood slowly, exactly the point. His own face, lighter than Kelly-Ann's, would sail through those cameras the way Adrien sailed through the photo software, and he would never once feel the machine fail him.

He opened his chat window before he could talk himself out of it.

"hey. the photo app can't find your face. any of them."

Three dots appeared, then stopped, then started again. "yeah it does that on my phone too. I just stopped using it."

"it found Adrien in two seconds. even with his hood up."

"I know."

He typed and deleted three sentences, each one more explanatory than the last, each one sounding, in his head, like he was delivering news from a country she lived in. Finally he pasted the link to the study and added only: "I want to put this in the project. Not your face thing, the study. Ms. Lim said one of our themes could be a sidebar if it connects."

Kelly-Ann replied with a single line: "my theme is geology."

He stared at it, sensing he'd missed something. Then: "put it in the geology sidebar. the software is sediment. it settles who it wants and hardens." He worried it sounded like one of Adrien's poetry attempts, a swerve into bathos right when she needed him to be practical. He was about to apologize for the sentence when she sent a burst of laughing emojis and then, "okay that's actually good. write it. I'll check it tomorrow."

He wrote it. He kept the numbers exact, exactly as the study had them, and described what he had watched happen on his own screen without embellishment, and did not claim to know why the gap existed, only that it did. His mom knocked and set a plate of toast at his elbow without a word, because she had learned not to interrupt him mid-project, and he ate it one-handed while arranging the final slide.

Adrien messaged at eleven, having seen the draft in the shared folder: "montane shots look insane. also what's this about error rates?"

"read the link," Anthony wrote. "tell me if I got anything wrong."

"you didn't. tested it myself. my face, instant. put in a photo of my cousin, nothing." A pause, then: "should we ask Ms. Lim if the whole class can test it?"

Anthony looked at the finished file, at the blank boxes still visible in his raw folder where Kelly-Ann should have been, forty-one empty rectangles like unmarked doors.

"Yeah," he typed. "First thing Friday. I'll bring the projector cable."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
The smell hit Isaac before the door did: cardamom, ghee, the wet iron of rain on his grandfather's coat hanging in the hall. His grandmother's house sat two streets from the gurdwara, and on the morning of the celebration the whole place had been turned into an anteroom, shoes piled by the door like offerings nobody had planned.

"Everyone eats there today," his grandmother said, pressing a paper bag of prasad into his hands. "You're bringing your friend, yes? The tall one?"

Gael was the tall one. Isaac had invited him a week ago, mostly to prove something, though if he paused to introspect, which he avoided doing, he wasn't sure whether the thing being proven was to Gael or to himself. His own attendance had thinned over the last year. He still covered his head in the hall, still sat where he was told, but he'd stopped praying somewhere along the way without deciding to, the way you stop noticing a poster on your bedroom wall.

Gael arrived at the grandparents' house in a stiff new shirt, holding a box of store-bought biscuits as if it were a passport. "I didn't know what you bring," he said. "To a temple. Is that even the word?"

"Gurdwara," Isaac said. "And you don't bring anything. That's kind of the point." He took the biscuits anyway, because his grandmother would press them on Gael later with tea, and refusing would have started a negotiation neither of them could win.

They walked over together, and Isaac felt a presentiment he couldn't justify, a tightness like the moment before a test you studied for and still expect to fail. What if Gael asked him a question he couldn't answer? What if the answer was that Isaac didn't believe any of it anymore, and the hall full of people who did would see that on him like a stain?

The shoe line inside was long. Then they climbed the carpeted stairs, scarves borrowed from a bin at the landing, and Isaac watched Gael's face as the hall opened up: the canopy, the singers, the men and women and children, and then, down the side corridor, the langar already running, rows of people sitting on the floor on long mats while volunteers moved between them with steel buckets of dal and rice.

"Everyone eats," Isaac said quietly. "Free. Vegetarian, doesn't matter who you are, what religion, nothing. Everybody sits on the floor, same level." He'd said it once before, he remembered, in the eighth grade, to a teacher who had asked about his holidays. He'd been prouder of it then. Now the sentence felt like something he was carrying for someone else, heavy at the handles.

There was a flashback then, uninvited: Isaac at seven, sitting cross-legged beside his grandfather in exactly this corridor, his legs going numb, complaining. His grandfather hadn't scolded him. He'd only said, "Look down the row," and Isaac had looked, and seen a man in a suit and a man in torn sneakers eating from the same steel thali, and had not understood what he was seeing, only that his grandfather wanted him to see it. His grandfather was in the kitchen now, ladling, his rolled sleeves dark with steam. That was the man's whole argument, Isaac thought, delivered without a word in forty years: the ladle, the floor, the row.

Gael, it turned out, had his own reason for coming. "My dad," he said as they sat down with their plates, "he says religion is just crowd control, and I want to be able to say I checked. Like, actually checked." He said it with an incisive flatness that Isaac recognized as armor. "So far the crowd control includes really good dal."

They ate. The dal was very good. A woman across the mat, older, her dupatta pinned with a safety pin that had lost its shine, caught Isaac staring into the middle distance and nudged a bowl of yogurt toward him without a word. He took some. The floor was hard in a way that felt deliberate, his legs folded under him, his plate warm on his palm, and he tried to hold two thoughts at once: that he no longer believed what the singers were singing, and that he believed completely in the row of people eating together, in its dumb unglamorous equality, and that he could not yet tell whether those were the same belief or opposite ones. His grandfather would say they were one. Gael's father would say neither counted. Isaac suspected the honest answer was that he didn't know yet, and that not knowing was allowed, even here, maybe especially here, where nobody had asked him for a credential at the door.

Afterward, in the corridor, his grandfather came out of the kitchen still holding the ladle, saw the two of them, and beckoned. "You," he said to Gael. "You washed dishes before?"

"Never in my life," Gael said.

His grandfather looked at Isaac, one eyebrow up, and held out the ladle to the boy who had brought his friend, as if to ask, and you? Isaac rolled his sleeves and followed them both through the kitchen door.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle described each virtue as a mean between two extremes; courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness.
story:
Stella had been sitting with the same cold latte for forty minutes, waiting for Zaynab, and rehearsing. Not the apology exactly, because she wasn't sure she owed one, but something adjacent to it, a way of saying I'd do it again but not like that. The coffee shop smelled of burnt espresso and the lemon cleaner the cashier was pushing around the floor in slow, doubtful arcs, as if the mop itself were reluctant.

Zaynab came in at four, right on time, which somehow made it worse. She ordered a tea she didn't touch and sat down across from Stella with the careful posture of someone entering a country she might have to leave quickly.

"Hi," Stella said.

"Hi."

"Thanks for coming."

"You said please twice in the text. Three times if you count the prayer hands."

At the robotics meeting on Tuesday, Stella had stood up in front of the whole team and said that the code Zaynab submitted for the competition was largely copied from an open-source repository without attribution, and that if they got caught, the whole team would be disqualified. It was true. It was also, in Mohammad's word, brutal. Zaynab had gathered her laptop and left, and the team had spent the remaining hour not looking at one another, and the coach had asked Stella afterward, quietly, whether there might have been a better moment. Stella had said, at the time, that there was no good moment for that kind of thing, only avoided ones.

"You humiliated me," Zaynab said now. Her voice was even, which was somehow more damning than shouting.

"You took the code," Stella said. "That part isn't in dispute, right?"

"You could have texted me. You could have said, fix it before Friday. Instead you stood up like you were delivering a verdict."

"I panicked. The submission closed in an hour."

"You didn't panic. Panicking is quiet. You performed."

Stella turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer, a small ceremonial gesture that propitiated no one, least of all herself. She wanted to say that Zaynab's shortcut had put everyone's work at risk, that responsibility wasn't a private matter when the consequences weren't, but she could hear how it would land, like a speech, and speeches were what had got her here.

Before Zaynab arrived, Mohammad had come by the table on his way out, milk-froth on his sleeve, and offered the only comfort he had. He was taking a philosophy elective, and he'd been quoting it all week like a man who'd found a coupon. "Aristotle," he'd said, dropping into the chair for exactly ninety seconds. "In the Nicomachean Ethics, he said every virtue is a mean between two extremes. Like, courage sits between cowardice and recklessness." He'd pointed his spoon at her. "You wanted to be brave. Brave is in the middle. You overshot into reckless. That's the whole theory, basically. Anyway, I have a shift." And he'd left, smelling faintly of cardamom, having upended her week in under two minutes.

She'd been turning it over since. Not whether Mohammad was right about Aristotle, that was just a thing he'd read, but whether it fit her. If cowardice was saying nothing and losing the team's chance, and recklessness was saying it the way she had, then the middle existed somewhere, and she had missed it by standing up instead of pulling Zaynab aside. But there was something slippery in the middle too, she thought, because the middle could be an excuse, a place where you told yourself you'd chosen well when really you'd only chosen comfortably. Some trade-offs didn't come with a setting you could dial in. Some were just two bad options and a stopwatch.

"You're doing the face," Zaynab said. "The one where you're arguing with yourself and losing."

"I'm trying to figure out if I owe you an apology or an explanation."

"Wow. Menu options."

"Both, probably. Zaynab, if it happened again, I'd still say something. That part I don't regret. But the where and the how, in front of everyone, that was." She stopped. The word reckless felt too large, like wearing someone else's coat. "That was past the line. I went too far. I'm sorry for that."

Zaynab looked at her untouched tea, then out the window, where a man was attempting to parallel park a van with visible petulant disbelief, as though the parking spot itself had wronged him. Zaynab almost smiled. Stella watched the almost and clung to it.

"I fixed it," Zaynab said finally. "Wednesday morning. Attribution, comments, a note to the coach. He says we're fine." She wrapped both hands around the teapot lid and lifted it, put it back, accomplished nothing. "I didn't sleep that night. Not because of the disqualification."

"Because of everyone seeing."

"Because everyone saw, and you were right." She said it like it cost money. "Which is worse. So I don't know what I want from this conversation, honestly. I want to still be angry and I want us to be okay and those two things keep bumping into each other."

"That's the whole conversation," Stella said. "Those are the whole two things."

Zaynab finally poured the tea, and the spout dribbled, and she said a word she'd learned from her grandmother, and Stella laughed before she could stop herself, and Zaynab, after a moment, laughed too, the rapprochement arriving sideways, unannounced, the way it apparently does. Stella still didn't know where the line was, exactly, between brave and too much, whether it moved depending on the stakes or the person or the hour left on the submission clock. She suspected she would miss it again someday and have to sit in another coffee shop with another cold drink.

"So," Zaynab said, pushing the sugar bowl across the table, one small white bowl traveling between them like a treaty. "Are you going to tell Mohammad he was useful, or do we let him keep thinking he's only funny?"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The game had not started yet when Florence's younger cousin planted himself in front of the television with a bag of chips, but the pregame show had, and there was the field, impossibly green, with the yellow first-down line already stretched across it. The cousin, who was nine and held his opinions the way other people held torches, announced that the groundskeeper must have to repaint the line after every play. Florence, folded into the corner of her grandmother's recliner with her phone half-raised, said nothing at first. She had watched football at this house every autumn of her life, and she had never once wondered about the line.

Her grandmother's living room filled the way it always did, by drift. Her father took the good couch, her uncle took the armchair nobody else wanted, and Maxim and Ingrid arrived at halftime of the earlier game with a grocery bag of oranges and the news that Ms. Chatterjee, their old English teacher, had been seen jogging past the gas station in atracksuit. Ingrid peeled an orange in one unbroken spiral, which mesmerized the cousin so thoroughly that he forgot the line for almost ten minutes. Then a punt, a return, a commercial, and the line appeared again, and he was back on it. "They paint it that fast?" he said. "That's not possible. Somebody has to run out there with a machine."

Florence typed with her thumb. The answer came up before the players had even broken the huddle, and she read it twice, because the first reading felt like a magic trick described after the fact. "It's not on the field," she said. "It's computer-drawn. It first showed up on ESPN on September 27, 1998. A company called Sportvision did it."

The cousin turned around slowly, as though she had told him the moon was a sticker. "But the players walk over it," he said. "I've seen them step on it." Maxim leaned forward out of the beanbag, interested now despite himself; he had thought the same thing until roughly a year ago and had never had the nerve to ask. "It's on the screen," Florence said. "Only on the screen. The field is just grass." Her uncle said something about witchcraft. Her father said that in his day they had to listen to the announcer tell you where the marker was, and you simply believed him, and the room absorbed that the way rooms absorb old grievances, without argument.

Ingrid, who wanted to be a journalist and collected facts the way other people collected ticket stubs, wanted to know whether the players saw it during the game. Florence said she didn't think so, and then corrected herself, said she didn't actually know, and the not-knowing sat in her strangely. It was like learning that a door she had walked through a thousand times had never once been locked. Or not like that, either. She tried out the thought that the line was a kind of metonymy, the screen standing in for the whole invisible apparatus of measurement that the actual game depended on, chains and markers and men crouching along the sideline, none of which the broadcast bothered to show. She didn't say this out loud. She was fairly sure it would come out wrong, and besides, the cousin had moved on to whether the players could see the score.

The game itself tightened in the third quarter. Her grandmother, who had been in the kitchen making a soup that smelled of dill and patience, came in and stood behind the couch with her arms crossed, watching, and it was her grandmother who yelled first when the receiver dropped the ball on the goal line. Florence found she was watching differently now. When the chain crew ran out to measure, she watched them instead of the ball. When the yellow line glowed across the fifteen, she thought: that is an opinion. Not a lie, exactly, but a decision about what to show, made by somebody in a truck, and the whole family was rearranging its hope around it.

The cousin, meanwhile, had gone quiet in the way that preceded either tears or schemes. At the two-minute warning he asked whether, if the line was computer-drawn, they could draw it in the wrong place, and nobody had an answer for him. Maxim said probably. Her uncle said they'd never do that. Ingrid said the word "probably" again, slower, like she was tasting it. Florence held her phone without typing anything. She had the fact, the whole of it, and the fact had opened onto a room larger than itself. She thought of Ms. Chatterjee standing at the whiteboard in April, saying that the interesting questions were never the ones you could settle, and she had rolled her eyes then, and she owed her, she supposed, a small apology now.

Her team lost by a field goal. The living room emptied in stages, her uncle first, then her father checking the lock on the screen door out of habit even though it was October and still warm. The cousin fell asleep against the good couch with orange peel stuck to one knee. In the kitchen, washing the soup pot because her grandmother's wrists were bad, Florence mentioned the line again, the date and the company, and her grandmother said she remembered the first time she'd seen it, 1998, and had complained to Florence's grandfather that the broadcasters were going to ruin the game for purists. "And did they?" Florence asked. Her grandmother considered the pot, the window, the dark yard beyond it.

"Somebody indigent could have fed a family for a season on what that machine cost," she said, "and I still yell at the line like it can hear me." She dried her hands and went to wake the boy.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
The temple smelled of incense and fried sesame balls, which Levi considered an unfair combination, because it made it impossible to be solemn while hungry. His mother had dragged him to the Lunar New Year service by promising it would take an hour, and it had already taken forty minutes of his life he would never recover, mostly spent standing while old men in gray cardigans chanted. Now the hall had emptied into the courtyard, where lanterns swung overhead and his little cousin Ruby was crouched on a bench, stuffing cash into a red envelope with the concentration of a bomb technician.

Levi drifted over, mostly because Issac and Marisa were at the tea table and Marisa had already beaten him at arm wrestling twice that afternoon. Ruby held up the envelope, sealed and crisp, and announced, "For Grandma's friend's grandson. He's six. I'm giving him forty dollars because I'm six times older than him plus some."

"Wait." Levi caught her wrist before she could tuck the envelope into her coat pocket. Forty dollars. Something snagged in his memory, a fragment from a unit on Chinese customs Mr. Liu had covered in world history, back when Levi had been paying more attention to Issac's doodles of sharks. He could picture Mr. Liu holding up a red envelope, could almost hear the sentence, but the actual content had been filed somewhere unreachable, behind the sharks.

"It's my money from my piggy bank," Ruby said, in the tone of a lawyer resting her case.

"I know. Hold on." Levi scanned the courtyard. Mr. Liu was by the incense burner, pouring tea for an auntie, and the service bell would ring again in ten minutes, at which point everyone filed back inside and the gift would be handed over at the door, because that was the ritual, that was the deadline. Levi left Ruby guarding the envelope like a dragon and cut across the courtyard, weaving between a man carrying a whole roast pig and two kids sword fighting with incense sticks.

"Mr. Liu. Red envelopes. There's a number you're not supposed to give."

Mr. Liu raised an eyebrow over his teacup. "There are several things one should not give. Clocks, for instance. White flowers. Sharp objects."

"Numbers. It's a number." Levi was sweating despite the cold. "You said it in class. I wasn't listening, which is on me, but it's important now, in the next ten minutes."

Mr. Liu set down the cup and looked genuinely amused, which did nothing to assuage Levi's panic. "You were not listening, so you want me to lecture a second time, for free, at a party."

"Consider it extra credit."

"Consider it," said Mr. Liu, "a riddle. What did your grandfather say when he chose his apartment number? Or when your mother picked a wedding date?" He turned back to the auntie, clearly enjoying himself, and Levi stood there feeling like a fish that had been shown the water and blamed for not drinking it.

Marisa appeared at his elbow with a sesame ball, half of it already in her mouth. "You look like you failed a quiz."

"I did fail a quiz. Six months ago. Retroactively." Levi told her the situation, and she chewed thoughtfully and said, "My grandma refuses to say it out loud. Our floor in her building goes three, then five." She held up four fingers, then folded one down. "Four. The word for four sounds like the word for death. So amounts with a four in them, that's a no. Forty is like handing someone a little death."

Levi stared at her. "You've been sitting on this the whole time?"

"You never asked. Also Issac bet me you'd come over here panicking. Detente is off, I'm collecting."

"That's tautological, by the way," Issac said, arriving with two more sesame balls, one visibly for himself. "You bet on him panicking and then watched him panic. That's not prophecy, that's just Levi."

They hurried back to the bench, where Ruby had not moved, as instructed, though she had licked her thumb and pressed it onto the envelope seal twice for extra security. Levi crouched down. "Change the forty to fifty. Or thirty. The number four is bad luck in a red envelope. Four sounds like death, so you skip it. Ask Mom if you don't believe me."

Ruby narrowed her eyes. "Then why did Mr. Liu teach it?"

"He didn't, technically. Marisa did."

"Marisa's grandma lives on a floor that doesn't exist," Ruby said, which was a fair summary, and Levi watched her tear open the envelope, count out the offending bills with enormous dignity, and substitute two crisp twenties from her other pocket. She smoothed the paper with the heel of her hand and held the envelope up to the lantern light, checking, he realized, that no four could possibly survive inside.

"There," she said. "Pure fifty. That kid is going to be so lucky he'll probably choke on it."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
On Monday Ms. Aydín handed Nathan a binder and said the one-act was his, and by Thursday he had learned that actors do not naturally stand where you want them to. He had also learned that "naturally" was a word he should stop using. The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and the stage, though flat, kept producing arguments about geography.

"Why is the back called up?" Raquel asked during the second rehearsal, standing where he had pointed and frowning at it. "This floor's flat as a math test. It's not up anywhere." She'd done a summer at the community theatre downtown, which was the only credential anyone in the room had.

"It's flat now," Jaskaran said, not looking up from his script. "It wasn't always." Nathan waited for more, because Jaskaran had a way of dropping half a fact and then checking whether you deserved the other half. "Upstage means away from the audience," he said finally. "Downstage means toward it. The words come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience." He shrugged, as if embarrassed by his own usefulness.

Nathan wrote it in the margin of his blocking notes and then, that night, sat with the notebook open on his bed, recalibrating everything he had planned. He had put the confrontation between Raquel's character and the mother in the upstage corner because it felt distant, and it turned out he had stumbled into the right choice by accident, which bothered him more than being wrong would have. He liked knowing why. The problem was that knowing why had a cost he hadn't anticipated.

He noticed it at Friday's run-through. He had blocked every entrance, every cross, every turn, and the actors moved through his map like students taking a test they hadn't studied for: accurately, joylessly. Raquel hit her mark and then stood in it, waiting. The mother, a sophomore whose name Nathan kept forgetting and then feeling terrible about, delivered her lines to a spot six inches left of Raquel's face because that was where the blocking said to look. When he called a break, Raquel didn't sit down. She came to the edge of the stage.

"You're directing us like traffic," she said. "Left, right, stop, go. At the community theatre my director used to say this whole bromide about how blocking should serve the story, and I rolled my eyes every time, but Nathan, he wasn't wrong. He just said it too much."

"I have notes," Nathan said. "Written notes. All of them."

"That's the problem."

He wanted to defend the notes. He had made them at eleven at night with diagram arrows, and they were good, they were careful, and being careful was the only thing he knew how to be. But he looked out past Raquel at the empty house, the folding seats, the aisle where Ms. Aydín would sit on Monday with her clipboard, and he thought about how the whole auditorium was arranged to look at them, all of it sloping, in a sense, toward this flat floor. The stage wasn't neutral. Nothing about it was.

"Run the scene again," he said. "Just the two of you. Ignore my notes. Find your own way to stand."

The mother glanced at Raquel, uncertain. Raquel nodded once, and something in her shifted, the mercurial thing that made her the best actor in the grade and the hardest person to direct, and they began. The mother came in downstage, close to where the audience would be, and Raquel retreated upstage a step, then another, letting the distance itself say what the argument was about, and Nathan watched from the tenth row with his notebook open and his pen not moving. When it ended, the silence lasted three full seconds before anyone breathed.

"That," he said, standing up. "Do exactly that. Can you do exactly that?"

"Probably not," Raquel said. "That kind of thing doesn't repeat on command."

"Then we'll find it again on Monday. I'll write down where you stood, and you can ignore it if it stops being true."

Raquel laughed, and the mother laughed too, and Ms. Aydín's clipboard sat on the piano bench where she'd left it, blank for now. Nathan walked up onto the stage and stood in the spot Raquel had chosen, looking out at all those empty seats.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy.
story:
The parking lot of the synagogue smelled of wet cedar, and Isabella sat in the passenger seat of her mother's car with a photocopied page in her lap, mouthing words she did not yet own. Tonight was the congregational Friday night dinner, the first her family had attended since her grandmother stopped cooking for it, and Rabbi's assistant had asked Isabella, of all people, to say the blessing over the wine. She was seventeen. She had never led anything at a table larger than four.

"Borei p'ri hagafen," she whispered, and the Hebrew slid around in her mouth like a stone she couldn't get comfortable under her tongue. She tried it again. The car windows fogged around her, and she thought, not for the first time, that there was something strange about rehearsing holiness in a parking lot, next to a cart of folding chairs and a puddle shaped like Australia.

Her phone buzzed. Deegan, who had known her since seventh grade and had come tonight mostly for the free food and partly because Isabella had begged. "You still in the car?" the message said. "People are staring at your mom through the window like she's a hostage."

Inside, the social hall had been transformed by tablecloths and someone's ambitious idea about candles. Max was already there, setting out little plastic cups of grape juice with the gravity of a person defusing bombs. Max had grown up doing this, had chanted the blessings at family dinners since before losing a first tooth, and Isabella watched the way his hands moved without thought, and wondered whether fluency like that could ever be borrowed, or whether it had to be grown.

"Kiddush," Max said when she asked, holding up one of the cups. "That's what the blessing is called. My grandfather used to make me do it at every festival meal, or Friday night, whatever came first." He said it lightly, the way you'd name a breed of dog, and she filed the word away like something warm carried in a closed fist.

Here was her problem, and it was not the Hebrew, though the Hebrew was hard. It was that her grandmother, in the hospital in October, had gripped Isabella's wrist and said, "You'll do it now," and Isabella had said yes, and had not understood until later that yes was a contract. Her grandmother had led the family's Sabbath dinners for forty years, standing at the head of the table with her chin lifted, her voice cracked and certain. In the flashback that visited Isabella now, she was eight years old, transfixed by the candlelight moving across her grandmother's face while everyone at the table fell silent, and she had thought that the silence itself was the blessing, that the words were only the doorway into it.

Now the doorway was hers and she didn't know the way through. Two voices argued in her, politely, like guests. One said: you memorize it, you say it correctly, you stand up straight, because the blessing marks the day as holy and getting it right matters, and correctness is a kind of respect. The other voice, quieter and more melancholic, said: your grandmother never got it perfectly right, she swallowed half the words, and everyone at that table would have followed her off a cliff. Which was it, then, the rectitude of the practiced syllables, or the plain fact of standing up in front of people you loved?

Ms. Mendoza, who lived two doors down and turned out to be the woman in charge of the evening, found Isabella standing frozen beside the juice table. "You're the one doing the wine blessing?" she asked, and when Isabella nodded, Ms. Mendoza didn't offer advice. She just straightened one candle that had burned crooked and said, "My mother led everything too. It's heavier than people tell you." Then she moved off to argue with a coffeemaker.

They sat down. The room went quiet in that gathering way, chairs scooting, napkins unfolding into laps, and Isabella felt her pulse in her throat. Deegan, across the table, gave her a look that meant go on. Max raised his cup slightly, an almost invisible encouragement.

She stood. She lifted the cup, and the words came out not perfectly, one of them stumbled, and somewhere behind her a small child laughed at nothing. And then she found the thread of it again, the ancient sentences her grandmother had carried, and when she said the blessing over the fruit of the vine, she heard her own voice do it, hearthigh and unsteady and entirely hers. The whole table answered Amen, and the sound of it moved through the hall like weather.
