Afterward, Deegan helped her carry the empty cups to the kitchen, and Isabella said, half to herself, "I don't know if I did it the right way or the right way." Deegan, who was not Jewish and had followed the whole evening with the fascinated attention of a traveler, said, "You mean there's a difference?"

"Yes," Isabella said. "No. I don't know yet." She stacked the cups upside down, the way her grandmother used to, having learned it from her without ever being taught. Outside the window the parking lot had gone dark, and the cedar smell came in when someone opened the door. Her mother was still at the table, talking to Ms. Mendoza, laughing at something, and Isabella watched her for a moment through the kitchen doorway.

"There's a festival coming next month," Deegan said. "Are you doing it again?"

Isabella rinsed the last cup and set it on the towel to dry. "Ask me when I'm walking to the car."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
story:
Vanessa had taped the graph to the fence with packing tape, because the wind kept lifting the corners and she wanted Alishba to see the whole century at once. The line climbed in small sawtooth steps, dipping and rising, dipping and rising, then bending steeply upward after 1950 like a road deciding against the mountain and going over it instead.

"Say it to me again," Alishba said, sitting cross-legged on the dead patch of grass near the compost bin. "But this time like I'm someone who failed chemistry."

"Sunlight comes through, hits the ground, the ground warms up and sends heat back toward space," Vanessa said, moving her hands like she was smoothing a bedsheet over the air. "Some gases let the sunlight in but catch the heat on the way out. Carbon dioxide is one of them. More of it, more heat held near the surface."

"That's it? That's the whole thing people fight about?"

"That's the part I can explain. The fighting part is separate."

Alishba squinted at the fence. "So why does the line wiggle instead of just going straight up?"

Vanessa knew the answer had something to do with the diurnal breathing of forests and the turning seasons, plants drawing the gas down in summer and releasing it in winter, but she had promised Ms. Mokoena she would not memorize her way through this. "The wiggles are the planet breathing," she said. "The bend in the line is us."

Behind them, the screen door slapped shut, and Ms. Mokoena came out carrying two glasses of lemonade and a folded newspaper she set on the picnic table without comment. She had lived next door since Vanessa was nine, had watched her learn to ride a bike on this same strip of lawn, and had volunteered, a week ago, to quiz Vanessa before the qualifying exam for the state climate literacy team. Only two students from their school could advance. Vanessa had not yet told Alishba that the second candidate was Alishba herself.

"Give me the numbers," Ms. Mokoena said.

"There aren't any yet. The graph is in parts per million, and I can read the shape, but the exam wants history too, and I keep getting the history wrong." Vanessa turned the printout over, where she had scrawled a timeline with half of it crossed out. "Everyone talks like climate prediction started with computers, with satellites, with the big models. I said that in practice yesterday and Ms. Mokoena, the marker wrote 'check this.'"

"You should check it," Ms. Mokoena said, and drank her lemonade.

Alishba pulled out her phone. "No signal back here by the bins," she said, and stood, walking toward the house with the phone held up like a lantern. Vanessa watched her go and felt the shape of the thing she was withholding settle somewhere under her ribs. Alishba had been studying too. Alishba had said nothing about it either. They had been friends since sixth grade and had apparently, without a word, become rivals.

When Alishba came back, her face had changed. "Okay, this is actually wild," she said. "The prediction is way older than computers. In 1896, a Swedish scientist named Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled. Eighteen ninety-six. Before airplanes. Before anyone had a screen at all."

Vanessa looked at the fence, at the sawtooth line, and did the arithmetic she had been avoiding. Arrhenius had done it with paper and patience, and everyone since had mostly been checking his work. "So when I said it started with computers, I wasn't just wrong, I was wrong in a way that matters," she said slowly. "Because if the first estimate came that early, then every year since is another year it could have been acted on. The graph isn't only a record of carbon. It's a record of what we knew and when."

"I hadn't thought of it like that," Alishba said.

"Neither had I." And this was the amalgam Vanessa had been circling all week without naming it: the science was simple enough to say with your hands over a bedsheet of air, and the history was simple enough to say in one sentence about a Swedish man with a pencil, and yet she had treated them as two separate subjects, graph in one notebook, dates in another, when the real thing, the thing worth saying aloud at an exam or anywhere else, was both at once. She was also honest enough, standing there, to admit what stayed uncertain for her: whether knowing early had ever moved anyone, whether it would move her, whether a person who could explain the mechanism and read the line was any different from a person who couldn't, if neither of them changed anything.

Ms. Mokoena set down her glass. "Vanessa," she said, "I graded your practice exam. I've been carrying it around all morning deciding whether to show you before the qualifier or after."

She unfolded the newspaper on the picnic table, and inside it was the exam sheet, and at the top, in the red marker Vanessa recognized from school, was a score high enough that only one student in the county had ever gotten one like it. The twist was not the score. The twist was the name printed beside the score, because Ms. Mokoena had graded both practice exams, both candidates, and had said nothing for a week, and the second name on the page was not Alishba's.

"It's Lucien," Ms. Mokoena said. "He registered last month. You two have been studying in my backyard and neither of you thought to mention him." Alishba was already reaching for her phone again, and the wind lifted the corner of the graph off the fence, and Vanessa pressed it flat with both hands.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Particle physicists claim a discovery only at 'five sigma', meaning there is less than a one-in-a-million chance that a random fluctuation alone would produce a signal that strong.
story:
Hayden set his laptop on the cleared end of the dinner table, angling the screen so the graph faced his father, who was still spooning rice onto his plate. The graph showed two wobbling lines with a small, stubborn gap between them.

"So I ran it again," Hayden said. "Third time. The effect is still there, but it's small."

His father chewed for a while, the way he did when he was deciding whether something was worth taking seriously. "How small?"

Hayden tapped the trackpad. "See the error bars? The gap is inside them. If you squint, it looks like something. If you don't, it looks like noise." The kitchen smelled of burnt garlic from the sauce his mother had left on the stove a minute too long; she was at the sink now, scraping a pan, and the scrape of metal on metal filled the pause where his father's answer should have been.

"Then it's nothing," his father said.

"It's not nothing. It's three times in a row."

Sabine, who had come over to work on the history project and had been absorbed into dinner without anyone deciding it, looked up from her noodles. "Three times in a row of what?"

Hayden turned the laptop toward her. "I'm testing whether plants grown near the speaker with low-frequency sound germinate faster than the ones in the quiet box. I measured sixty seeds in each group. The speaker group came out ahead every run." He caught himself before he said the word, then said it anyway. "Slightly ahead."

"Sixty seeds is a lot of seeds," Sabine said.

"It's nothing. Particle physicists won't even call something a discovery until it hits five sigma." His father's fork stopped halfway. Hayden kept going, faster now, because he had read the page four times last night and the numbers had stuck. "Five sigma means there's less than a one-in-a-million chance that a random fluctuation alone would produce a signal that strong. Less than one in a million. Everything below that, they just keep measuring."

His father set the fork down. "You're comparing bean sprouts to the Large Hadron Collider."

"I'm comparing being sure to being not sure. The scale is different. The idea isn't."

From the sink, his mother said, without turning around, "The Vishnu seedlings on the balcony died because you left the tray in the sun, so maybe don't lecture anyone on certainty." That got a laugh out of Sabine, and Hayden felt his ears go hot, but he didn't close the laptop. He opened the spreadsheet instead and slid it down the table, past the dish of yogurt, past his father's glass, until it bumped the salt shaker.

"If you think it's nothing," Hayden said, "then replication shouldn't scare you. Mr. Mansour has the same kind of setup in his greenhouse. He offered. If I run it there, with his seeds, his soil, and the effect disappears, I was wrong and I'll write that down. If it shows up again, it's four times, in two places."

His father looked at the spreadsheet for a long moment. Hayden watched him find the column where one tray had been forgotten in the sun, the run he had almost deleted and, in the end, only marked. The kitchen had gone quiet enough that Hayden could hear the tick of the oven cooling and, underneath it, his own pulse in his ears. He was aware, in some corner of his consciousness, that he had practiced this argument in the shower that morning, and also that practicing it and standing here with the rice getting cold were not the same thing at all.

"You marked the bad run," his father said.

"I almost deleted it. That felt like cheating."

"It would have been." His father took the laptop and scrolled, slowly, through all three runs, and Hayden watched his face do something complicated, something between reluctance and the reluctant beginning of interest. "When I was your age I fudged a lab report once. Changed a six to an eight. The teacher never caught it. I still think about it more than I think about most things I got caught doing."

"That's a profligate use of guilt," Sabine said. "Spending it all on a two."

His father smiled at her, briefly, and pushed the laptop back across the table. "Mansour's greenhouse, then. But if it disappears, you write the whole thing up anyway. The null result."

"That's the plan," Hayden said, and it was half true. The plan until ten minutes ago had been to find a way to make the effect bigger. It occurred to him, sitting there with the graph glowing between the salt and the yogurt, that a result you protected wasn't a result at all; it was a wish with numbers on it.

Later, when the plates were stacked and Sabine had absconded with the last of the yogurt cup into the living room to finish her half of the history timeline, Hayden stood at the window with his phone and texted Mr. Mansour. Are you still serious about the greenhouse? He typed it, deleted it, typed it again, and added: Not trying to prove I'm right. Trying to find out.

The reply came while he was rinsing the pan his mother had abandoned: Saturday morning, come early, I'll put the kettle on.

Hayden set the phone face-up on the windowsill, where the kitchen light caught the screen, and went back to the warm water and the burnt smell still hanging in the air. Outside, the balcony tray sat empty in the dark, sixty little pots of maybe waiting for Saturday.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
story:
Sienna spread her notes on the flat rock at the pond's edge and weighed the corners down with two stones and Farah's shoe. The science fair results had gone up that morning: her entry, a working model of cellular respiration built from aquarium tubing and painted wooden mitochondria, had a red sticker beside it, which meant rejected, not even a category placement. She had carried the model to the pond anyway because her mother would not be home until six, and because she did not want to look at it in her bedroom.

Farah sat cross-legged on the grass, eating sunflower seeds and reading the judge's comment sheet over Sienna's shoulder. "They say the pathway is 'inaccurately simplified.' That's all. Two words and you're out."

"I left out the cycle part," Sienna said. "The part where the thing that gets broken down gets rebuilt and goes around again. I couldn't fit it on the board, so I cut it." She picked up her pen and drew a hexagon on the back of her hand, glucose, then an arrow, then the small oval she had painted black a hundred times. "Glucose gets split, the pieces get stripped for electrons, the electrons go down a chain, and the chain pumps protons, and the protons flowing back through a motor make ATP. That part I had. It's the middle I faked."

Mr. Novák came down the path with his dog, an old spaniel that went straight to the water and stood there without drinking. He lived two doors from the school and walked this loop every afternoon at four. "Red sticker," he said, when he saw the board propped against a willow. "I had one of those. Mine was a compost thermometer."

"Did yours say 'inaccurately simplified'?"

"Mine said 'ambitious beyond scope,' which I believe was the same thing." The dog lowered itself into the shallow water up to its elbows. He sat down on the next rock, not close, the way he usually did, as if the pond had assigned seats.

Sienna flipped through her notes, hunting for the middle she had cut. She had copied a diagram from the textbook two weeks ago, a circle of eight reactions, arrows chasing their own tails, and underneath it a name she had not read carefully: the citric acid cycle, Hans Krebs. Farah leaned over. "Who's Krebs?"

"That's what I'm going to find out." Sienna had signal at the pond some days and not others; today she had one bar. She searched the name, and the phone screen loaded a biography in slow pieces, paragraphs arriving like a tide. She read half of it silently, then aloud. "Nature rejected his 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle. He published it in Enzymologia instead."

"What's Nature?"

"Journal. The one everybody wants. They turned him down." She scrolled further. "He got the Nobel Prize later, for the cycle. The one I cut off my board."

Farah spat a seed shell into the grass. "So the judges are Nature and you're Krebs."

"I'm not Krebs. Krebs figured out the thing. I built a model of it out of tubing and got the tubing wrong." But she said it without heat, and she kept the phone out, and after a minute she said, "They rejected the real thing and printed mine for a lesser reason. Those aren't the same, but they rhyme."

Mr. Novák had been skipping stones, badly, the spaniel watching each failure with interest. He turned around. "When I got my red sticker, my teacher told me the rejection was the universe testing me. I have never liked that. Sometimes a thing is just turned down, and you have to decide separately whether to go on."

"That's the part I'm working on," Sienna said. She pulled the model over and unscrewed one end of the aquarium tubing. Inside, her painted oval had a gap where the cycle should have looped back on itself, a deliberate blank she had covered with a paper label reading "and so on." She peeled the label off and let the wind take it toward the cattails.

Libby arrived then, bike helmet still on, having seen the red sticker on the results board and ridden straight out. She looked at the stripped model, at the open notes, at the phone still glowing with Krebs's face. "Are you fixing it?"

"I don't know yet. It's a lot of encumbrance to carry around, a rejected board and my whole pride, and I'd rather put both down and see what's actually there." She took the pen and, on the inside of the oval, began drawing the loop back: the four-carbon piece picking up a two-carbon piece, going around, losing carbons, arriving where it started so it could go again. Farah held the phone light against the rock as the sun dropped.

"Is that right?" Libby asked, watching the arrows close the circle.

"It's right enough to redo. Whether it's right enough to enter again next year, I don't know. I'll decide that later." She drew the last arrow home and tapped the closed ring twice with the pen. The spaniel shook itself dry, and water came off it in a wide arc across the grass.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
story:
The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and Mr. Reyes's coffee, which he made too strong and drank anyway, impervious to the winces of everyone else in the house. Jackson sat across from him at the table with a spiral notebook open to a page of numbers, and between them lay a paper bag of rolls his grandfather had picked up that morning before the drive.

"You still working on that?" Mr. Reyes asked, nodding at the page. He was a neighbour who had retired into the apartment above theirs and had somehow habituated himself to their kitchen table, arriving at seven with groceries the way other people arrived with gossip.

"I'm trying to figure out how far we went yesterday," Jackson said. He tapped the column of figures. "Grandpa let me call out the speedometer every minute on the way to the lake. I wrote it all down. Sixty, sixty-two, fifty-eight, fifty, fifty-four. Like that, the whole way."

"You could just read the odometer."

"I did. That's the thing. I want to see if I can get there without it."

Nada had put the idea in his head two weeks ago, in the library, and he kept circling back to it. She was a year ahead of him, already through calculus, and she'd drawn him a curve on scrap paper and shaded the space beneath it with quick hatch marks. "The integral," she'd said, "is the area under the curve." He'd thought she was being abstract for the pleasure of it, the way she sometimes was, and he'd said so, and she'd laughed and told him he'd see.

He saw, partially, now. On the page he had drawn axes and marked the minutes along the bottom and the speeds up the side, and the points he'd recorded made a jagged line when he connected them. The area underneath was a band of graph-paper squares, some full and some cut through by the line. He'd started counting them, then stopped, because counting felt like the dumb way, the way Toby would do it, and Toby got the same answers Jackson did but never cared why.

"That looks like a lake," Mr. Reyes said, tilting his head at the shaded region.

"It's a velocity-time graph." Jackson said it before he could worry about sounding like a textbook. "Speeds on this side, minutes along there. If the speed were constant, distance would be easy, speed times time. But it kept changing. So I'm chopping the trip into pieces. Every minute, I take the speed and multiply by one minute, and I add them all up."

Mr. Reyes set down his cup. "Like a stack of little rectangles."

"Right. Narrow ones. The narrower I make them, the closer I get." Jackson drew the rectangles in, one per minute, and where the speed was sixty for a whole minute the rectangle was clean, and where it dipped and rose the top of the rectangle cut the line or left a gap, and he sat looking at those errors, those small triangles of wrongness, and understood for the first time that the integral was what you got when the wrongness got small enough to stop mattering. The area under the velocity-time graph over the time interval was the displacement, the actual distance between start and finish.

He added the column twice. Fifty-one point four miles. He found the odometer reading in his phone, from a photo he'd taken of the dashboard before they left and after they parked, because even then he'd suspected he'd want to check. Fifty-one point one.

"Close?" Mr. Reyes asked, watching his face.

"Three tenths of a mile off." Jackson leaned back. "That's the part I don't get yet. Whether the leftover is the error I can shrink, or something I'm leaving out entirely." He thought of his grandfather's hands on the wheel, how the old man had gunned it getting onto the highway and gone slow past the farm stand, as though speed were a language he was translating from. "Mr. Reyes, when you drive, do you ever think about the fact that the whole trip is just this, this adding up?"

"Son, when I drive I think about my knees and the price of gas." He pushed the bag of rolls across the table. "Eat something before school. Your grandfather bought those for you, not the counter."

Jackson took one and kept the notebook open beside it, drawing the rectangles narrower, half a minute wide, then imagining them thinner still, his pencil hovering over the gap where the curve bent away. Nada's voice came back to him, her hatch marks, her certainty. He texted her a photo of the page and set the phone face down next to the crumbs.

The toast was cold but he ate it anyway, and before he left he tore the page out carefully, along the perforation, and folded it into his back pocket, where the corners would soften all day against the bus seat.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The Saturday market smelled of wet cardboard and fried dough, and Samantha carried her failed loaf in a cloth bag like evidence. Two nights ago she had pulled it from the oven, dense as a brick and crumbly where it should have torn soft, and her mother had said nothing, which was worse than saying something. She had promised the family a real dinner tonight, soup and bread, bread that she made, and now the bread was a humiliation in a bag and she had one morning to fix it.

She found Mr. Abdi at his stall first, because his table of flour sacks was the closest thing the market had to an answer. He was weighing something on a brass scale, and when she unpacked her loaf and set it between the jars of honey he stopped weighing and looked at it a long moment. "You didn't knead it enough," he said, "or you kneaded it wrong," and then a customer wanted walnuts and he had to turn away, so that was all she got from him.

Cadence appeared at her elbow with a cup of cider, torpid with heat even at ten in the morning. "Is that the loaf? God. It looks like a fossil." Samantha put it back in the bag. Cadence's family bought bread from a bakery, the artisanal one by the river, and Samantha had spent a lot of the summer being quietly superior about that, saying that the bakery had found a way to commodify the one thing that used to be free, which Cadence found pretentious and probably was. Samantha had announced, back in July, that bread was patrimony, that her grandmother had made it every Friday and she was going to learn, and now her patrimony sat in a bag like a rock.

"Marcel's over there talking to the egg people," Cadence said. "He made bagels last month. They were actually good." Marcel's bagels had been good; Samantha had eaten two of them and felt something complicated about it. They found him comparing cartons, and he came willingly enough, dusting chalky fingerprints on his jeans.

Samantha laid the loaf out again on the edge of a crate. "It didn't rise like the picture. It came out heavy and it crumbles when I cut it." Marcel turned it over and pressed his thumb into the crust. "My first ones were like that," he said. "I looked it up for hours. Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water." He said the names slowly, like he'd practiced them once for someone. "So the flour and the water do part of it on their own. But kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger, and the bread chewier. I was stopping too early. Ten minutes felt like eternity so I quit at five." He shrugged. "Once I actually kept going, the dough changed under my hands. You can feel it happen."

Samantha turned that over. Her recipe had said knead until smooth and elastic, eight minutes maybe, and she had gone by the clock and by her own boredom, and the dough had stayed shaggy and she had decided that was fine. "So it's not the oven. It's not even really the recipe. It's that I stopped." Marcel nodded. Cadence, who had been listening with her chin on her fist, said, "So you just have to be more stubborn than the dough," and Samantha laughed, a real one, the first since the loaf came out wrong.

She bought five kilos of Mr. Abdi's stone-ground flour, which emptied most of her wallet, and carried it against her hip through the rest of the market while she picked up what dinner needed: carrots, a knuckle of ginger, three onions from the farmer who never bagged them for you, just let you hold the produce first. At home her mother had left a note about being back at six. The kitchen was hers until then.

She mixed the flour and water first and let them sit, because Marcel had said the two proteins only needed water to start forming gluten, and waiting felt like doing something even though it looked like doing nothing. Then she turned the dough onto the counter and pushed and folded, pushed and folded, and at five minutes her shoulders burned and at eight minutes she wanted to stop again, and she thought about the bakery by the river and about her grandmother's hands, which she had never actually watched make bread, only claimed, and she kept going. Somewhere past ten minutes the surface went from shaggy to smooth, and when she pressed a fingertip into it the dent slowly filled itself back in, and she stood there with flour on her forearms feeling the dough push against her palm like something alive.

She set it near the warm window to rise, put the soup on, and while the dough climbed over the rim of its bowl she wrote at the bottom of her grandmother's card, in pencil, "longer than you think," and underlined it twice. When her mother came through the door at six and asked what smelled so good, Samantha wiped her hands on her apron and said, "Sit down in half an hour. And don't cut it until I do."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
The whole living room smelled like burnt popcorn because Brynn had refused to accept the microwave's judgment and run it a second time. Mya had the good armchair, the one by the window, and she was guarding it with her legs folded under her like a drawbridge raised. On the screen, the game was tied, and Dellaway, the visiting team's shooting guard, had just made his fifth shot in a row.

"He is flaming," said her uncle from the couch, gesturing with a chip as though presenting evidence to a jury. "You do not leave Dellaway alone when he's like this. That's just basketball."

"That's just a story you tell yourself," Mya said, and immediately regretted the phrasing, because Brynn sat up from the floor with the particular delight of someone who has found an argument to ride all night.

"Oh, here we go. Mya read one article."

"Two articles, actually." She reached for her phone, then put it down, because she could feel the shape of what she knew without checking. "There was this study in 1985, by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They looked at whether players actually shoot better after making shots, and they said no. They called the hot hand an illusion."

"An illusion," repeated her uncle, in the tone of a man being told the moon was fabric.

"An illusion," Mya confirmed. "Streaks that look like streaks are just a coin coming up heads a bunch of times, and people see a pattern because people are extremely good at seeing patterns that aren't there. My chem teacher says the same thing about us seeing faces in the periodic table." She shrugged. "But then in 2018 these other researchers, Miller and Sanjurjo, went back and reanalyzed it, and they found a statistical flaw in the original work. And they found evidence of streak shooting. Real streaks. So the hot hand might be true after all."

The room took this in the way a room takes news during a timeout, which is to say half of it did. Simran, cross-legged on the rug with a plate of the unburnt popcorn, raised a hand like they were in class. "So which one's right?"

"That's the annoying part. I don't know. Both of them, kind of, in different ways." Mya unfolded one leg and pointed it at the screen. "The 1985 people were right that we see streaks everywhere, even where there's nothing. The 2018 people were right that sometimes there's something. The problem is that when you're watching, you can't tell which time is which."

"So what you're saying," said Brynn slowly, savoring it, "is that the scientific answer is 'it depends,' which is the answer to every question you have ever given about anything."

"It is not the answer to everything."

"What's a monomer?"

"A molecule that bonds to other molecules to form a polymer, which has nothing to do with basketball and everything to do with my quiz tomorrow, which is why my flashcards are on your foot."

Brynn looked down, moved the flashcards, and grinned. On the screen the game had restarted, and the announcers were doing the thing announcers do, which was building a cathedral out of one man's evening. Dellaway is in a zone, one of them said. You can feel it in the building. Mya's uncle nodded along with religious calm, and Simran, who had been quiet, leaned toward the TV as if to get a better read on the truth of the matter.

Dellaway got the ball in the corner, wide open in a way that made the whole room groan in advance. His uncle was already half standing, arm raised, the chip abandoned. The shot went up, hung there, and Mya realized she was holding her breath, which she felt was a betrayal of everything she had just said. The ball clanked off the back rim. Two players from her uncle's team wrestled for the rebound.

"See," her uncle said, sitting back down with enormous dignity. "Cold hand. The illusion goes both ways, sweetheart."

"That's not what either study said, and also you changed sides four minutes ago."

"A canny fan changes with the evidence."

"That's not evidence, that's one shot!" Mya was laughing now, and so was Simran, and Brynn had begun narrating the rebound battle in the voice of a nature documentary. Somewhere in the fourth quarter the game would end and someone would be right for reasons that had nothing to do with being right, and tomorrow Mya would walk into chemistry knowing polymers cold and knowing this only partly. Dellaway got the ball again, and this time he didn't hesitate.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide level measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record.
story:
Isla spread the printout across her grandmother's kitchen table on Saturday morning, weighting the corners with a jar of marmalade and a sugar bowl. The graph showed a red line climbing in shallow sawteeth across sixty years, and by Monday she had to stand in front of her class and explain what the line meant, why it rose, why the sawteeth themselves mattered. She had promised Ms. Gupta a rehearsal in her head by Sunday night, and she had promised herself something vaguer, that she would actually understand it rather than memorize it, though she could not yet say where the difference lay.

Her grandmother set down two mugs of tea and bent over the paper with the interest of someone inspecting a dress pattern. "Where does it cross that horizontal line," she asked, tapping the graph where a thin black line ran flat across the page, marked with a small 400. "The one you keep circling."

"That's the part I have to get right," Isla said. She traced the red line with her finger until it nudged past the black one. "On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million. First time in the record." She said it the way she had said it into the mirror that morning, and it sounded, here in the warm kitchen, less like knowledge and more like something she was carrying for someone else.

Her grandmother sat down slowly. "Four hundred of what, now?"

"Parts per million. Out of every million molecules of air, four hundred are carbon dioxide." Isla paused. She had read that it sounded small and was not, but she did not want to say that part wrong, so she reached for the comparison Ms. Gupta had used, a blanket, thick enough to change things even though it is thin compared with the bed. "The gases trap heat. Sunlight comes in, and the warmth tries to leave, and the carbon dioxide keeps some of it from getting out. More gas, thicker blanket." She stopped, waiting to be corrected, but her grandmother only nodded, turning her mug in her hands.

Isla had not expected to be practicing here. She had planned to rehearse at Melody's house on Saturday, with Melody timing her and Adele pretending to be a hostile audience member who asked impossible questions, a game they had invented during the history presentations in the spring. But Melody's little brother had come home from school with a fever, and their mother had texted that Isla should stay away until they knew what it was, some antigen the doctors were testing for, the message said, and so Isla had taken the bus one stop further, to the house with the crooked gate, and found herself explaining the atmosphere to her grandmother instead.

The radio on the counter murmured through the noon news, something about a ceasefire in a country whose name Isla could not have found on a map without checking, negotiations between sectarian factions that had agreed, at least for the weekend, to stop shelling each other. Her grandmother reached over and turned the volume down without comment, as though quieting an argument in another room.

"Go on, then," her grandmother said. "From the beginning. Pretend I know nothing, because I very nearly don't."

Isla began again, and this time she went slower. She talked about sunlight and about the surface of the earth warming and sending heat back up, about molecules of carbon dioxide catching that heat and returning it, so that the world holds a little more of its warmth than it used to. She showed how the red line wavered up and down each year in small teeth, and said the teeth were the seasons, the forests of the northern hemisphere breathing in and out, one breath per year, and she watched her grandmother's face when she said it, because that was the moment the whole thing had enraptured her when Ms. Gupta first drew it on the board, the idea that you could see the planet breathing in a line of data.

"And this is one mountain," her grandmother said. "One place, measuring the whole sky."

"One observatory on a volcano in Hawaii. But the air mixes, so it comes out about the same everywhere." Isla put her finger back on the graph, on the exact point where the red teeth crossed the flat black line. "May 9, 2013. Before that day, the daily average had never passed 400 in the whole record." She heard herself say it plainly this time, and it sat differently in her mouth, not a memorized fact but a thing that had happened on a day, a real day with weather, while she was nine years old and unaware of it.

"I would have been seventy-one," her grandmother said. She looked at the rising line for a while, the sawteeth marching upward past the crossing point and beyond the edge of the page. "And it kept going after that."

"It kept going," Isla said. "That's the part I haven't figured out how to end with. Melody wants me to close with something hopeful, and Adele says I should just show the line and let it be bad, and I keep going back and forth. Because it's true that people built things that changed it, and it's true that the line kept going anyway, and I don't want to pretend one of those isn't real just so my ending is clean."

Her grandmother pulled the sugar bowl aside so the corner of the graph curled up free, and pressed it flat again with her palm. "Then don't end clean," she said. "Stand there and tell them what you told me, including the part you haven't settled. When I was your age I thought a person had to be finished to speak. Nobody told me the unfinished ones were the only ones worth listening to."

Isla copied that into the margin of her notes, beneath the circled 400, and underlined it twice. On Monday, she decided, she would ask the class to hold up their hands if they had been alive in May 2013, and she would count the hands.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A 2013 study led by John Cook examined 11,944 climate paper abstracts and found that 97.1 percent of those taking a position endorsed human-caused global warming.
story:
The bus dropped them outside the geosciences building at nine, and Maelie counted the windows instead of listening to Samy, who was still going on about the debate they'd had in the parking lot. "I'm just saying it's fifty-fifty," Samy said, holding the door for the line of seniors from Ms. Carvalho's class. "Half the scientists say it's us, half say it's natural. That's what my uncle keeps posting." Maelie had argued back with something she'd half-remembered, some statistic about consensus, and Samy had asked, twice, where she'd gotten it, and she hadn't been able to say. That was the thing that stung. She hated quoting a number she couldn't trace.

Ms. Carvalho gathered them in the lobby beneath a skeleton of some arboreal fern, taller than the stairwell, its black fronds fanned against the skylight. "We split into threes," she said. "Maelie, Samy, Remi, you're with the climate group on the third floor. Ask questions. Don't touch the mass spectrometer." Remi grinned and mouthed mass spectrometer back at Maelie like it was a spell.

The third floor smelled of burnt coffee and cardboard. A grad student with paint on her wrists handed them clipboards and put them to work sorting printed abstracts into folders, and only after ten minutes of this did Maelie see what the folders were. Climate papers. Hundreds of them, maybe thousands, their titles running from the technical to the incomprehensible. "What's this for?" she asked. The grad student said a professor in the department kept the file for teaching, a copy of a coding exercise from an old study, and pointed at a poster rolled above the desk. "Unroll that if you want the context. Carefully."

Remi got one end and Maelie the other, and the poster crackled open against the wall. It was a schematic of a study, the kind that adumbrated its whole structure in boxes and arrows before a single sentence of prose: abstracts read, positions coded, results tallied. At the top, in the grad student's handwriting for some seminar, was the citation. A 2013 study led by John Cook. Maelie read the line beneath it twice. It had examined 11,944 climate paper abstracts. Her eye went straight to the end of the sentence, the way it did when she checked a grade. Of the abstracts that took a position, 97.1 percent endorsed human-caused global warming.

"Ninety-seven percent," Remi said over her shoulder. "Of the ones that took a position. That's the part people skip."

"I didn't skip it, I didn't know it," Maelie said. She was still holding her edge of the poster. Somewhere behind the sentence was the shape of the work itself: thousands of abstracts, read and coded, not by one person but by a method, checked by other hands. She thought of her statistic from the parking lot, the one she'd thrown without provenance, and understood that it had been a veneer of knowledge, a smooth surface over nothing. "Samy," she said. "Come look."

Samy came, arms folded, and read. "Okay," Samy said. "One study."

"No, that's the point," Maelie said, and heard herself building it as she spoke, testing each plank before she stepped on it. "Eleven thousand nine hundred and forty-four papers. That's not one result, that's thousands of papers, and the study just counted them. And it's one count among others, other people have gone and counted again. That's how you know a thing in science, not because somebody smart says it, but because it keeps showing up when different people look." She paused, honest with herself and then out loud. "I don't understand the climate part, the mechanisms, none of that. I can't explain why it's happening. But the split you described, half and half, that part isn't real, and I can say that now because I've seen where the number comes from."

Samy looked at the poster a long moment, then took out a phone and photographed it, the flash whitening the citation for an instant. "I'm sending this to my uncle," Samy said, which was not agreement, but it wasn't nothing either. "He'll say Cook was biased." "Then that's the next question," Maelie said. "Who checked his work." The grad student, overhearing, laughed once and said, "Now you're doing it," and handed Maelie another stack of abstracts.

They sorted in a quiet row by the window until Ms. Carvalho called the class down. On the bus home Remi slept against the glass and Samy typed to the uncle, and Maelie watched the campus trees go by, counting them out of habit, and got to sixty-three before the city took over.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
The restaurant smelled of garlic and scorched coffee, and Luca had spread his homework across the small table by the window as though the newspaper might bolt if he didn't pin it down. Jesse slid into the seat across from him, stole a fry, and read the headline upside down.

"You're still doing this?"

"Friday," Luca said. "Mr. Fitzgerald makes us read one article out loud and summarize it. In Italian." He said the last part quietly, because the family at the next table had already looked over once.

Jesse ordered a milkshake and watched Luca trace the first line of the article with his pen, mouthing words. Luca's mother had enrolled him in the evening class without asking him, and for six weeks he had hated it with a private, patient hatred, the kind that portends a longer argument nobody has started yet. But the language was beginning to open to him the way a lock does, a little at a time, and he couldn't decide whether that felt like being let in or being taken.

Aryan arrived with his own article, glossy and folded, from the same class. He was the best in the group and knew it, though he carried it lightly, the way an apologist carries an argument he has already won. "Did you practice?" he asked.

"Twice," Luca said. He hadn't practiced once. He had instead spent an hour on the train deciding that summaries were an antiquated form, that nobody condensed anything anymore, that the whole assignment was a ceremony without a purpose. He had almost convinced himself.

The waiter brought the milkshake. Luca read the article aloud to the table, slowly, and the sound of his own voice in the restaurant made the words feel both more real and more fragile than they had on the train. Then Aryan asked him to summarize, and Luca began the way he always began, with the first thing he understood, which was the story about the bridge that had reopened in the north of the country.

"It's a bridge story," Aryan said. "From Spain."

"What?"

"Look at the front of the article. Before the first sentence." Aryan tapped the small line of type at the top, the one Luca had skipped every week, the way you skip a doorway you assume leads nowhere.

Luca looked. Two words, a city name, set off before everything else, printed ahead of the first sentence like a signature at the top of a letter. He checked his own article. The same thing: a city, then the story. Every article in the paper began that way, he realized, city first, printed before the first sentence, naming the place where the story had been reported. Six weeks of reading and he had never once seen the door.

"So the bridge is Spanish," Jesse said, delighted.

"The bridge is in the north," Luca said. "Of Spain. Not of anywhere I said." He felt his ears go hot. In his head he had built the entire summary on the wrong country, and it had held together perfectly, which was the part that frightened him. It would have held together out loud, too. Mr. Fitzgerald would have nodded along.

He tried again. He put the city back where it belonged, at the beginning, and rebuilt the summary around it, and this time the sentences came slower and truer. Aryan listened with his arms folded, not correcting, which was worse and also better. When Luca finished, Aryan said, "Now it's a bridge story."

Jesse raised the milkshake in a toast to the bridge, wherever it was. Luca folded the newspaper and, out of a habit he hadn't known he had, checked the front of the menu on the table, the part above the first sentence, the part everyone skips.

"Madrid," he said. "Even the menu's from Madrid."
